Filip Fryš and Jan Kotrbatý Address: Charles University, Faculty of Mathematics and Physics, Mathematical Institute of Charles University, Sokolovská 49/83, 186 00 Prague, Czechia Email address: filip.frys@matfyz.cuni.cz Email address: kotrbaty@karlin.mff.cuni.cz
Date: September 17, 2026
Abstract.

We consider two higher-order generalizations of the Godbersen conjecture for mixed volumes of convex bodies, which were first proposed by Schneider in 2000. First, we establish the conjectures in several special cases, in particular in low dimensions. Second, we prove that certain consequences of the conjectures hold. More precisely, we define a higher-order version of the unbalanced difference body and prove related weighted inequalities, generalizing previous results of Artstein-Avidan and Putterman. Finally, we introduce higher-order analogs of unbalanced joins of convex bodies considered by Artstein-Avidan, Einhorn, Florentin, and Ostrover, prove the corresponding volume bounds, and propose conjectures that interpolate between the higher-order Godbersen conjectures and a conjecture due to Fáry and Rédei.

2020 Mathematics Subject Classification
52A40, 52A39

1. Introduction

The Godbersen conjecture asserts that the geometric invariants associated with a convex body in Euclidean space via mixed volumes with the opposite body are maximized by simplices. Dating back to the 1938 thesis of C. Godbersen [5], it has been one of the longest-standing open problems in convex geometry, and until very recently, only special cases and consequences of the conjectured inequality have been known.

A notable example of such a consequence is the classical Rogers–Shephard inequality [20, 21]. It states that, among all convex bodies K⊂ℝnK\subset\mathbb{R}^{n} of fixed positive volume |K||K|, the volume of the corresponding difference body DK={k−l:k,l∈K}DK=\{k-l\,:\,k,l\in K\} is maximal for simplices; more precisely

(1) |D​K|≤(2​nn)​|K|,\displaystyle|DK|\leq{2n\choose n}|K|,

where equality holds if and only if KK is a simplex.

It is a remarkable fact and a cornerstone of the Brunn–Minkowski theory that the Lebesgue measure on ℝn\mathbb{R}^{n} polarizes when restricted to the class 𝒦⁡(ℝn)\mathcal{K}(\mathbb{R}^{n}) of convex bodies. In other words, there exists a (unique) function V:𝒦​(ℝn)n→ℝV:\mathcal{K}(\mathbb{R}^{n})^{n}\to\mathbb{R}, called the mixed volume, that is symmetric, multilinear and satisfies V⁡(K,…,K)=|K|V(K,\dots,K)=|K|. Here linearity is with respect to the Minkowski addition K+L={k+l:k∈K,l∈L}K+L=\{k+l\,:\,k\in K,l\in L\} and scaling r​K={r​k:k∈K}rK=\{rk\,:\,k\in K\} by a non-negative factor r≥0r\geq 0. Let us emphasize that although one can scale KK by any r∈ℝr\in\mathbb{R}, the mixed volume is not homogeneous for r<0r<0.

Observe that D​K=−K+KDK=-K+K is the Minkowski sum of KK with its reflection −K=(−1)​K-K=(-1)K about the origin. Expanding the left-hand side of (1) by multilinearity and the right-hand side using (2​nn)=∑j=0n(nj)2{2n\choose n}=\sum_{j=0}^{n}{n\choose j}^{2}, Godbersen [5] and later independently Makai Jr. [19] conjectured that the inequality holds terms by term:

Conjecture 1.1 (Godbersen conjecture).

Let 0≤j≤n0\leq j\leq n. For any K∈𝒦⁡(ℝn)K\in\mathcal{K}(\mathbb{R}^{n}) one has

(2) V⁡(−K⁡[j],K⁡[n−j])≤(nj)​|K|.V\big(-K[j],K[n-j]\big)\leq{n\choose j}|K|.

Moreover, if 0<j<n0<j<n and dimK=n\dim K=n, equality holds if and only if KK is a simplex.

The conjecture holds trivially for j∈{0,n}j\in\{0,n\} and follows easily for j∈{1,n−1}j\in\{1,n-1\} from the properties of the Minkowski asymmetry measure, see §2.4. In particular, it is true in dimensions n≤3n\leq 3. Godbersen [5] further verified (2) in the case when KK is of constant width, i.e., when D​KDK is a Euclidean ball. Much more recently, Conjecture 1.1 was verified for anti-blocking convex bodies by Artstein-Avidan, Sadovsky, and Sanyal [3], and Sadovsky [22] subsequently extended this result to the class of locally anti-blocking bodies, see [3, 22] for precise definitions of these classes. Very recently, the second-named author and Mouamine [12], using a surprisingly simple argument based on the monotonicity of mixed volume, proved (2) for general convex bodies and established the characterization of equality cases for convex polytopes.

The proof of (2) given in [12] is directly motivated by the renewed attention recently attracted by the so-called higher-order generalization of the Rogers–Shephard and related inequalities, see, e.g., [7, 14, 16, 8, 15, 17, 9, 18, 26, 13] and reference therein. This concept goes back to Schneider [23] who considered for general p∈ℕp\in\mathbb{N} the higher-order difference body Dp​K=−Δp​K+KpD_{p}K=-\Delta_{p}K+K^{p}, where Δp:ℝn→ℝp​n\Delta_{p}:\mathbb{R}^{n}\to\mathbb{R}^{pn} is the diagonal embedding, and proved the following generalization of (1):

(3) |Dp​K|≤(n​p+nn)​|K|p\displaystyle|D_{p}K|\leq{np+n\choose n}|K|^{p}

with equality if and only if KK is a simplex (unless dim(K)<n\dim(K)<n). Note that, strictly speaking, Schneider [23] used a different sign convention for Dp​KD_{p}K, see §2.2 for more details.

Expanding the left-hand side of (3) in terms of mixed volumes and using an appropriate combinatorial identity for (n​p+nn){np+n\choose n}, one may again conjecture that the inequality holds term by term. This was done recently by the second-named author [11].

Conjecture 1.2 ([11, Conjecture 1.2]).

Let p∈ℕp\in\mathbb{N} and 0≤j≤n0\leq j\leq n. For any K∈𝒦⁡(ℝn)K\in\mathcal{K}(\mathbb{R}^{n}) one has

(4) V⁡(−Δp​K​[j],Kp​[n​p−j])≤(nj)​|K|p.V\big(-\Delta_{p}K[j],K^{p}[np-j]\big)\leq{n\choose j}|K|^{p}.

Moreover, if p≥2p\geq 2, j>0j>0, and dim(K)=n\dim(K)=n, equality holds if and only if KK is a simplex.

Conjecture 1.2 can be further refined using Kp=ι1​K+⋯+ιp​KK^{p}=\iota_{1}K+\dots+\iota_{p}K, where ιi:ℝn→ℝp​n\iota_{i}:\mathbb{R}^{n}\to\mathbb{R}^{pn} is the inclusion into the ii-th factor of ℝp​n=ℝn×⋯ℝn\mathbb{R}^{pn}=\mathbb{R}^{n}\times\cdots\mathbb{R}^{n}. In this way one arrives at

Conjecture 1.3 ([11, Conjecture 1.3]).

Let p∈ℕp\in\mathbb{N} and j0,…,jp∈ℕ0j_{0},\dots,j_{p}\in\mathbb{N}_{0} such that j0+⋯+jp=nj_{0}+\cdots+j_{p}=n. For any K∈𝒦⁡(ℝn)K\in\mathcal{K}(\mathbb{R}^{n}) one has

(5) V⁡(−Δp​K​[n−j0],ι1​K​[n−j1],…,ιp​K​[n−jp])≤(n!)p(n​p)!​(nj0,…,jp)​|K|p.\displaystyle V\big(-\Delta_{p}K[n-j_{0}],\iota_{1}K[n-j_{1}],\dots,\iota_{p}K[n-j_{p}]\big)\leq\frac{(n!)^{p}}{(np)!}{n\choose j_{0},\dots,j_{p}}|K|^{p}.

Moreover, if p≥2p\geq 2, j0,…,jp<nj_{0},\dots,j_{p}<n, and dim(K)=n\dim(K)=n, equality holds if and only if KK is a simplex.

As pointed out to us by E. Putterman, Conjecture 1.3 was in fact already made in 2000 by Schneider, see [24, p. 537]. Schneider also explains that the problem dates back to the seminal paper of Janson [10] and attributes to Janson the proof of (5) in the special case p=n−1p=n-1 and j0=⋯=jn−1=1j_{0}=\dots=j_{n-1}=1, see [24] and Proposition 3.2 below. Recently, the second-named author [11, Theorem 1.4] proved that Conjecture 1.3 (and hence Conjecture 1.2) holds for the class of anti-blocking convex bodies.

1.1. Our results

In this paper, motivated by the previous developments in the classical case p=1p=1, we provide additional evidence for validity of the higher-order Godbersen conjectures. More precisely, we verify Conjectures 1.2 and 1.3 in some special cases and prove that certain potential consequences of the conjectures are true; moreover, we also formulate new conjectures, both weaker and stronger than Conjectures 1.2 and 1.3.

1.1.1. Special cases of the higher-order Godbersen conjectures

First, we prove Conjectures 1.2 and 1.3 for some specific values of the parameters jj and j0,…,jpj_{0},\dots,j_{p}, respectively. These results in particular imply that Conjecture 1.2 is true in dimensions n≤3n\leq 3 and Conjecture 1.3 for n≤2n\leq 2. Moreover, using Janson’s inequality mentioned above, the latter extends to dimension three, however without the characterization of equality cases.

Second, using a generalization of an argument due to Godbersen [5], we verify Conjectures 1.2 and 1.3 for low-dimensional convex bodies of constant width. Notice that, unlike in the case p=1p=1, (4) is not symmetric in jj and n−jn-j. Consequently, the argument works in general dimension only if j≤n2j\leq\frac{n}{2} in Conjecture 1.2. Along the way, we also observe that both conjectures are true for symmetric convex bodies (of any dimension). Although this is not difficult to see, it is not as obvious as for p=1p=1.

Third, we show that the higher-order difference body of a product body is the product of higher-order difference bodies and conclude that the validity of both conjectures is stable under the operation of taking cartesian products.

To summarize, our first main result is

Theorem 1.4.

The following special cases of Conjectures 1.2 and 1.3 are true:

  1. (a)

    Conjecture 1.2 holds for n≤3n\leq 3.

  2. (b)

    Conjecture 1.3 holds for n≤2n\leq 2. If n=3n=3, then (5) holds for any K∈𝒦⁡(ℝ3)K\in\mathcal{K}(\mathbb{R}^{3}).

  3. (c)

    Conjecture 1.2 holds for convex bodies of constant width if n≤6n\leq 6 or if j≤⌊n2⌋j\leq\lfloor\frac{n}{2}\rfloor.

  4. (d)

    Conjecture 1.3 holds for convex bodies of constant width if n≤3n\leq 3. If n∈{4,5,6}n\in\{4,5,6\}, then (5) holds for any K∈𝒦⁡(ℝn)K\in\mathcal{K}(\mathbb{R}^{n}) of constant width.

  5. (e)

    Conjecture 1.3 (and hence Conjecture 1.2) holds for symmetric convex bodies.

  6. (f)

    Fix p∈ℕp\in\mathbb{N}. If inequality (5) holds for Ki∈𝒦⁡(ℝni)K_{i}\in\mathcal{K}(\mathbb{R}^{n_{i}}), i=1,2i=1,2, then the cartesian product K1×K2∈𝒦⁡(ℝn1+n2)K_{1}\times K_{2}\in\mathcal{K}(\mathbb{R}^{n_{1}+n_{2}}) satisfies Conjecture 1.3, and analogously for Conjecture 1.2.

Let us point out that item (f) of Theorem 1.4 can be iterated and combined with other items as well as with the previously established case of anti-blocking convex bodies [11]. In this way we obtain the validity of Conjectures 1.2 and 1.3 for finite cartesian products of bodies from the corresponding classes.

1.1.2. Higher-order unbalanced difference bodies and weighted inequalities

As the Godbersen conjecture had long appeared out of reach, various consequences of it were studied as potential evidence in its favour. In a recent paper, Artstein-Avidan and Putterman [2] proved two different inequalities for weighted sums of mixed volumes V⁡(−K⁡[j],K⁡[n−j])V\big(-K[j],K[n-j]\big), that would follow at once from (2). One of them in particular implies that the Godbersen conjecture holds in a certain sense on average, cf. Corollary 1.6 below. Moreover, Artstein-Avidan and Putterman defined for a convex body K∈𝒦⁡(ℝn)K\in\mathcal{K}(\mathbb{R}^{n}) and general t∈[0,1]t\in[0,1] the unbalanced difference body

Dt​K:=−t​K+(1−t)​KD^{t}K:=-tK+(1-t)K

and conjectured the corresponding Rogers–Shephard-type inequality. They also showed that this conjecture, weaker than Conjecture 1.1 and subsuming (1) for t=12t=\frac{1}{2}, would imply both of their weighted inequalities.

Here we generalize the inequalities of Artstein-Avidan and Putterman [2] to the higher-order setting. We emphasize that although we list below for simplicity only the corresponding results related to Conjecture 1.2, we also obtain a precisely analogous set of statements related to the more general Conjecture 1.3. Our first result in this direction and the second main result of the paper is a direct generalization of [2, Theorem 4]:

Theorem 1.5.

Let p∈ℕp\in\mathbb{N}. For any K∈𝒦⁡(ℝn)K\in\mathcal{K}(\mathbb{R}^{n}) and t∈[0,1]t\in[0,1], one has

(6) ∑j=0ntj​(1−t)n−j​V​(−Δp​K​[j],Kp​[n​p−j])≤|K|p.\sum_{j=0}^{n}t^{j}(1-t)^{n-j}V(-\Delta_{p}K[j],K^{p}[np-j])\leq|K|^{p}.

If dim(K)=n\dim(K)=n and equality holds for some t∈(0,1)t\in(0,1), then KK is a simplex.

Clearly, Theorem 1.5 would follow from Conjecture 1.2 if the latter is true. Furthermore, integrating (6) with respect to tt over the interval [0,1][0,1] yields at once the following inequality, which generalizes [2, Corollary 5] and shows that (4) holds “on average”:

Corollary 1.6.

Let p∈ℕp\in\mathbb{N}. For any K∈𝒦⁡(ℝn)K\in\mathcal{K}(\mathbb{R}^{n}), one has

1n+1​∑j=0n(nj)−1​V​(−Δp​K​[j],Kp​[n​p−j])≤|K|p.\frac{1}{n+1}\sum_{j=0}^{n}{n\choose j}^{-1}V\big(-\Delta_{p}K[j],K^{p}[np-j]\big)\leq|K|^{p}.

Our third main result is a weighted inequality for the mixed volume of −Δp​K-\Delta_{p}K and KpK^{p} with different weights than in Theorem 1.5, generalizing [2, Theorem 7]. Note that a straightforward computation shows that also the following theorem would be implied by Conjecture 1.2:

Theorem 1.7.

Let p∈ℕp\in\mathbb{N}. For any K∈𝒦⁡(ℝn)K\in\mathcal{K}(\mathbb{R}^{n}) and t∈[0,1]t\in[0,1], one has

(7) ∑j=0ncn,p,j​(t)​V​(−Δp​K​[j],Kp​[n​p−j])≤|K|p,\displaystyle\sum_{j=0}^{n}c_{n,p,j}(t)V\big(-\Delta_{p}K[j],K^{p}[np-j]\big)\leq|K|^{p},

where

cn,p,j​(t)≔∑m=0n​p−j(n​p−mj)​(n​p)!​n!m!​(n​p+n−m)!​(1−t)m​tn​p−m.c_{n,p,j}(t)\coloneqq\sum_{m=0}^{np-j}{np-m\choose j}\frac{(np)!n!}{m!(np+n-m)!}(1-t)^{m}t^{np-m}.

If dim(K)=n\dim(K)=n and equality in (7) holds for some t∈(0,1)t\in(0,1), then KK is a simplex.

Finally, for any p∈ℕp\in\mathbb{N} and t∈[0,1]t\in[0,1] we define the higher-order unbalanced difference body corresponding to a convex body K∈𝒦⁡(ℝn)K\in\mathcal{K}(\mathbb{R}^{n}) as

Dpt​K≔(1−t)​Kp−t​Δp​K.D_{p}^{t}K\coloneqq(1-t)K^{p}-t\Delta_{p}K.

Notice that for p=1p=1 we recover the unbalanced difference body of Artstein-Avidan and Putterman, i.e., D1t​K=Dt​KD_{1}^{t}K=D^{t}K. In this connection, motivated by [2, Conjecture 2], we propose

Conjecture 1.8.

Let p∈ℕp\in\mathbb{N}. For any K∈𝒦⁡(ℝn)K\in\mathcal{K}(\mathbb{R}^{n}) with dim(K)=n\dim(K)=n and any t∈[0,1]t\in[0,1], one has

(8) |Dpt​K||K|p≤|Dpt​Sn||Sn|p,\displaystyle\frac{|D_{p}^{t}K|}{|K|^{p}}\leq\frac{|D_{p}^{t}S_{n}|}{|S_{n}|^{p}},

where Sn∈𝒦⁡(ℝn)S_{n}\in\mathcal{K}(\mathbb{R}^{n}) is an nn-simplex. If equality holds for some t∈(0,1)t\in(0,1), then KK is a simplex.

Observe that Conjecture 1.8 is trivial for t=0t=0 and t=1t=1, and holds for t=12t=\frac{1}{2} by Schneider’s inequality (3). Expanding both sides of (8) using multilinearity of mixed volumes, it is immediate that Conjecture 1.2 implies Conjecture 1.8. Moreover, we prove that even the weaker Conjecture 1.8 implies Theorems 1.5 and 1.7, extending the same phenomenon from the case p=1p=1 considered in [2] to general p∈ℕp\in\mathbb{N}, see Propositions 6.3 and 6.4, respectively.

As pointed out above, we also prove analogous results for the mixed volume of −Δp​K-\Delta_{p}K and ι1​K,…,ιp​K\iota_{1}K,\dots,\iota_{p}K, that is, related to Conjecture 1.3. More precisely, the analogs of Theorem 1.5 and Corollary 1.6 are Theorem 7.3 and Corolary 7.4, respectively. Theorem 1.7 is in fact proven as a special case of its analog in this more general setting, Theorem 7.6. Finally, we also define for each p∈ℕp\in\mathbb{N}, K∈𝒦⁡(ℝn)K\in\mathcal{K}(\mathbb{R}^{n}), and 𝒕=(t0,…,tp)∈ℝ+p+1\bm{t}=(t_{0},\dots,t_{p})\in\mathbb{R}_{+}^{p+1} satisfying ∑l=0ptl=1\sum_{l=0}^{p}t_{l}=1, the more general version of unbalanced higher-order difference body

Dp𝒕​K:=−t0​Δp​K+∑l=1ptl​ιl​K,D_{p}^{\bm{t}}K:=-t_{0}\Delta_{p}K+\sum_{l=1}^{p}t_{l}\iota_{l}K,

and propose Conjecture 7.7 analogous to Conjecture 1.8. To complete the analogy, we show in Propositions 7.8 and 7.9 that Conjecture 7.7 implies Theorems 7.3 and 7.6, respectively. Note that also all these results boil down to the corresponding results of [2] for p=1p=1.

1.1.3. Inequalities for higher-order unbalanced joins of convex bodies

Finally, we generalize to the higher-order setting the results of Artstein-Avidan, Einhorn, Florentin, and Ostrover [1] who considered the unbalanced join of KK and −K-K. More precisely, they proved a sharp upper bound on the volume of −t​K∨(1−t)​K=conv⁡(−t​K∪(1−t)​K)-tK\vee(1-t)K=\conv\big(-tK\cup(1-t)K\big) and proposed a related conjecture that interpolates between Conjecture 1.1 and a long-standing conjecture due to Fáry and Rédei [4].

Our main result in this direction is the following inequality that generalizes [1, Theorem 1.5]:

Theorem 1.9.

Let p∈ℕp\in\mathbb{N}. For any K∈𝒦⁡(ℝn)K\in\mathcal{K}(\mathbb{R}^{n}) with 0∈K0\in K and any t∈[0,1]t\in[0,1], one has

(9) |−t​Δp​K∨(1−t)​Kp|≤(1−t)n⁡(p−1)​|K|p,\displaystyle\left|-t\Delta_{p}K\vee(1-t)K^{p}\right|\leq(1-t)^{n(p-1)}|K|^{p},

If dim(K)=n\dim(K)=n and equality holds for some t∈(0,1)t\in(0,1), then KK is a simplex with a vertex at the origin.

A straightforward consequence of Theorem 1.9 is the following inequality which gives a somewhat weaker upper bound on the mixed volume of −Δp​K-\Delta_{p}K and KpK^{p} than conjectured by (4). For p=1p=1, the inequality reduces to [1, Theorem 1.4].

Corollary 1.10.

Let p∈ℕp\in\mathbb{N} and 0<j<n0<j<n. For any K∈𝒦⁡(ℝn)K\in\mathcal{K}(\mathbb{R}^{n}) one has

V⁡(−Δp​K​[j],Kp​[n​p−j])≤nn(n−j)n−j​jj​|K|p.V\big(-\Delta_{p}K[j],K^{p}[np-j]\big)\leq\frac{n^{n}}{(n-j)^{n-j}j^{j}}|K|^{p}.

Finally, we propose the following unbalanced Fáry–Rédei type conjecture, which generalizes [1, Conjecture 1.2]:

Conjecture 1.11.

Let p∈ℕ.p\in\mathbb{N}. For any K∈𝒦⁡(ℝn)K\in\mathcal{K}(\mathbb{R}^{n}) with dim(K)=n\dim(K)=n, and every t∈[0,1]t\in[0,1], there exists x∈Kx\in K such that

|−t​Δp​(K−x)∨(1−t)​(K−x)p||K|p≤|−t​Δp​Sn∨(1−t)​(Sn)p||Sn|p,\frac{\left|-t\Delta_{p}(K-x)\vee(1-t)(K-x)^{p}\right|}{|K|^{p}}\leq\frac{\left|-t\Delta_{p}S_{n}\vee(1-t)(S_{n})^{p}\right|}{|S_{n}|^{p}},

where Sn∈𝒦⁡(ℝn)S_{n}\in\mathcal{K}(\mathbb{R}^{n}) is a centered nn-simplex.

In Proposition 8.3 we show that Conjecture 1.11, if true, implies the inequality (4) in Conjecture 1.2. This generalizes [1, Theorem 1.3].

We point out that, for the sake of brevity, we again list here only the results obtained in the context of Conjecture 1.2, that is, related to the bodies −Δp​K-\Delta_{p}K and KpK^{p}. Analogous results corresponding to Conjecture 1.3 and to the bodies −Δp​K-\Delta_{p}K and ι1​K,…,ιp​K\iota_{1}K,\dots,\iota_{p}K are proven in Section 9. More precisely, the analogs of Theorem 1.9, Corollary 1.10, Conjecture 1.11, and Proposition 8.3 are Theorem 9.1, Corollary 9.2, Conjecture 9.3, and Proposition 9.6 respectively.

To conclude the introduction, let us emphasize that although the high-level strategy of the proofs of our main results introduced in §1.1.2 and §1.1.3 is in general motivated by the proofs of the corresponding results in the case p=1p=1 given in [2] and [1], respectively, the generalization to p≥1p\geq 1 often requires additional ideas and arguments beyond the basic case. This in particular implies to the inequalities involving the convex bodies −Δp​K-\Delta_{p}K and ι1​K,…,ιp​K\iota_{1}K,\dots,\iota_{p}K; notable examples are the proofs of Theorems 7.6 and 9.1.

2. Preliminaries

In this section, we summarize some basic facts from convex geometry. For more details, we refer the reader to [25]. Throughout the paper, we will consider Euclidean space ℝn\mathbb{R}^{n} equipped with the canonical Lebesgue measure |⋅||\cdot| and assume n≥2n\geq 2. We will denote ℝ+≔[0,∞)\mathbb{R}_{+}\coloneq[0,\infty) and ℕ0≔{0}∪ℕ\mathbb{N}_{0}\coloneq\{0\}\cup\mathbb{N}. We will denote by Bn⊂ℝnB^{n}\subset\mathbb{R}^{n} the closed Euclidean unit ball centered at the origin.

2.1. Convex bodies

A convex body is a nonempty, compact, and convex subset K⊂ℝnK\subset\mathbb{R}^{n}. The family of all convex bodies in ℝn\mathbb{R}^{n}, denoted by 𝒦⁡(ℝn)\mathcal{K}(\mathbb{R}^{n}), is closed under Minkowski addition

K+L:={k+l:(k,l)∈K×L}K+L:=\{k+l\,:\,(k,l)\in K\times L\}

as well as under scalar multiplication by r∈ℝr\in\mathbb{R}

r​K:={r​k:k∈K}.rK:=\{rk\,:\,k\in K\}.

When equipped with the Hausdorff metric

dH(K,L):=inf{r>0:K⊂L+rBn,L⊂K+rBn},d_{H}(K,L):=\inf\{r>0\,:\,K\subset L+rB^{n},L\subset K+rB^{n}\},

𝒦⁡(ℝn)\mathcal{K}(\mathbb{R}^{n}) becomes a locally compact, complete metric space.

The reflection of K∈𝒦⁡(ℝn)K\in\mathcal{K}(\mathbb{R}^{n}) about the origin is denoted by −K:=(−1)​K-K:=(-1)K. Similarly, for K,L∈𝒦⁡(ℝn)K,L\in\mathcal{K}(\mathbb{R}^{n}) and x∈ℝnx\in\mathbb{R}^{n}, we abbreviate K−L:=K+(−L)K-L:=K+(-L) and K±x:=K+{±x}K\pm x:=K+\{\pm x\}. A convex body K∈𝒦⁡(ℝn)K\in\mathcal{K}(\mathbb{R}^{n}) is said to be symmetric if −K=K+x-K=K+x for some x∈ℝnx\in\mathbb{R}^{n}; K∈𝒦⁡(ℝn)K\in\mathcal{K}(\mathbb{R}^{n}) is said to be of constant width if K−K=r​BnK-K=rB^{n} for some r∈ℝ+r\in\mathbb{R}_{+}.

We define the dimension of a convex body K∈𝒦⁡(ℝn)K\in\mathcal{K}(\mathbb{R}^{n}), written dim(K)\dim(K), as the dimension of the affine span of KK. We say that K∈𝒦⁡(ℝn)K\in\mathcal{K}(\mathbb{R}^{n}) is full-dimensional if dim(K)=n\dim(K)=n or, equivalently, int⁡(K)≠∅\inter(K)\neq\emptyset.

Let K1,K2∈𝒦⁡(ℝn)K_{1},K_{2}\in\mathcal{K}(\mathbb{R}^{n}). We define the join K1∨K2≔conv​(K1∪K2)K_{1}\vee K_{2}\coloneqq\textup{conv}(K_{1}\cup K_{2}) to be the smallest convex body containing both K1K_{1} and K2K_{2}. This definition extends naturally to finitely many convex bodies.

We will frequently make use of the following result due to Rogers and Shephard.

Lemma 2.1 ([21, Theorem 1]).

Let 1≤j≤n−11\leq j\leq n-1 and let E⊂ℝnE\subset\mathbb{R}^{n} be a jj-dimensional affine subspace. Then for any full-dimensional K∈𝒦⁡(ℝn)K\in\mathcal{K}(\mathbb{R}^{n}) one has

|PE⟂​K|⋅|K∩E|≤(nj)​|K|,|P_{E^{\perp}}K|\cdot|K\cap E|\leq{n\choose j}|K|,

where PE⟂P_{E^{\perp}} denotes the projection to the orthogonal complement of EE.

Moreover, equality holds if and only if for every a∈E⟂a\in E^{\perp}, the set K∩(E+ℝ+​a)K\cap(E+\mathbb{R}_{+}a) is obtained by taking the convex hull of K∩EK\cap E and one more point. In particular, if equality holds, then all nonempty sections K∩(E+a)K\cap(E+a), a∈E⟂a\in E^{\perp}, are homothetic.

Let us also recall the classical Brunn-Minkowski inequality.

Theorem 2.2 ([25, Theorem 7.1.1]).

For all K1,K2∈𝒦⁡(ℝn)K_{1},K_{2}\in\mathcal{K}(\mathbb{R}^{n}) and t∈[0,1]t\in[0,1] one has

|(1−t)​K1+t​K2|1n≥(1−t)​|K1|1n+t​|K2|1n.\big|(1-t)K_{1}+tK_{2}\big|^{\frac{1}{n}}\geq(1-t)|K_{1}|^{\frac{1}{n}}+t|K_{2}|^{\frac{1}{n}}.

Moreover, if dimK1=dimK2=n\dim K_{1}=\dim K_{2}=n, then equality holds for some t∈(0,1)t\in(0,1) if and only if K1K_{1} and K2K_{2} are homothetic.

Finally, for K1,K2∈𝒦⁡(ℝn)K_{1},K_{2}\in\mathcal{K}(\mathbb{R}^{n}) with dimK1=dimK2=n\dim K_{1}=\dim K_{2}=n and 0∈int⁡(K1)0\in\inter(K_{1}), and x∈ℝnx\in\mathbb{R}^{n}, we define the K1K_{1}-anisotropic distance as

dK1​(x,K2)≔min⁡{r≥0:x∈K2+r​K1}.d_{K_{1}}(x,K_{2})\coloneqq\min\{r\geq 0:x\in K_{2}+rK_{1}\}.

Observe that the function x↦dK1​(x,K2)x\mapsto d_{K_{1}}(x,K_{2}) is continuous. Furthermore, for r≥0r\geq 0, one has K2+r​K1={x∈ℝn:dK1​(x,K2)≤r}K_{2}+rK_{1}=\{x\in\mathbb{R}^{n}:d_{K_{1}}(x,K_{2})\leq r\}.

2.2. Higher-order difference body

Let p∈ℕp\in\mathbb{N}. Recall that the higher-order difference body of K∈𝒦⁡(ℝn)K\in\mathcal{K}(\mathbb{R}^{n}) is given by Dp​K:=−Δp​K+KpD_{p}K:=-\Delta_{p}K+K^{p}, where Δp:ℝn→(ℝn)p\Delta_{p}:\mathbb{R}^{n}\to(\mathbb{R}^{n})^{p} denotes the diagonal embedding, i.e., Δp​(x)=(x,…,x)\Delta_{p}(x)=(x,\dots,x) for x∈ℝnx\in\mathbb{R}^{n}. It is straightforward to verify that

Dp​K={(x1,…,xp)∈(ℝn)p:K∩(K−x1)∩⋯∩(K−xp)≠∅},D_{p}K=\left\{(x_{1},\dots,x_{p})\in(\mathbb{R}^{n})^{p}\,:\,K\cap(K-x_{1})\cap\cdots\cap(K-x_{p})\neq\emptyset\right\},

see [11, Proposition 3.1]. In fact, this was the original definition of Schneider [23] who, however, used the opposite sign convention, i.e.,

{(x1,…,xp)∈(ℝn)p:K∩(K+x1)∩⋯∩(K+xp)≠∅}=Δp​K−Kp.\left\{(x_{1},\dots,x_{p})\in(\mathbb{R}^{n})^{p}\,:\,K\cap(K+x_{1})\cap\cdots\cap(K+x_{p})\neq\emptyset\right\}=\Delta_{p}K-K^{p}.

Observe that if dimK=n\dim K=n, then 0∈int⁡(Dp​K)0\in\inter(D_{p}K). Indeed, if dimK=n\dim K=n, there exist ϵ>0\epsilon>0 and x∈int⁡(K)x\in\inter(K) such that x+ϵ​Bn⊂Kx+\epsilon B^{n}\subset K. Then for any w∈ϵ​Bnw\in\epsilon B^{n} one has x∈K−wx\in K-w which shows that (ϵ​Bn)p⊂Dp​K(\epsilon B^{n})^{p}\subset D_{p}K.

2.3. Simplices

Let 0≤k≤n0\leq k\leq n. A convex body K∈𝒦⁡(ℝn)K\in\mathcal{K}(\mathbb{R}^{n}) is called a kk-simplex (or just simplex) if K=conv⁡{v0,…,vk}K=\conv\{v_{0},\dots,v_{k}\} is the convex hull of affinely independent points v0,…,vk∈ℝnv_{0},\dots,v_{k}\in\mathbb{R}^{n}. We say that a kk-simplex conv⁡{v0,…,vk}\conv\{v_{0},\dots,v_{k}\} is centered if v0+⋯+vk=0v_{0}+\dots+v_{k}=0.

If Sn=conv⁡{v0,…,vn}⊂ℝnS_{n}=\conv\{v_{0},\dots,v_{n}\}\subset\mathbb{R}^{n} is an nn-simplex, there exist affine functions Aj:ℝn→ℝA_{j}\colon\mathbb{R}^{n}\to\mathbb{R}, j=0,…,nj=0,\dots,n, satisfying ∑j=0nAj=1\sum_{j=0}^{n}A_{j}=1 and Aj​(vi)=δi​jA_{j}(v_{i})=\delta_{ij} such that

Sn={x∈ℝn:Aj(x)≥0,j=0,…,n}.S_{n}=\{x\in\mathbb{R}^{n}\,:\,A_{j}(x)\geq 0,j=0,\dots,n\}.

We will need the following characterization of simplices, first proven for λ=1\lambda=1 by Rogers and Shephard [20] and later extended to λ∈(0,1)\lambda\in(0,1) by Artstein-Avidan and Putterman [2]:

Lemma 2.3 ([20, Lemma 4] and [2, Proposition 10]).

Let K∈𝒦⁡(ℝn)K\in\mathcal{K}(\mathbb{R}^{n}) with dim(K)=n\dim(K)=n, and let λ∈(0,1]\lambda\in(0,1]. If (λ​K+x)∩K(\lambda K+x)\cap K is homothetic to KK for all x∈int⁡(K−λ​K)x\in\inter(K-\lambda K), then KK is a simplex.

More precisely, we will use the following two easy consequences of Lemma 2.3:

Corollary 2.4.

Let p∈ℕp\in\mathbb{N} and 0<s≤t≤10<s\leq t\leq 1. If K∈𝒦⁡(ℝn)K\in\mathcal{K}(\mathbb{R}^{n}) with dim(K)=n\dim(K)=n is homothetic

  1. (a)

    either to K∩⋂i=1p(K−wi)K\cap\bigcap_{i=1}^{p}(K-w_{i}) for all (w1,…,wp)∈Dp​K(w_{1},\dots,w_{p})\in D_{p}K,

  2. (b)

    or to (t​K−w)∩s​K(tK-w)\cap sK for all w∈int⁡(tK−sK)w\in\inter(tK-sK),

then K is a simplex.

Proof.

Assume first that the condition (a) holds. If x∈K−Kx\in K-K, then K∩(K+x)≠∅K\cap(K+x)\neq\emptyset. Hence −Δp​(x)∈Dp​K-\Delta_{p}(x)\in D_{p}K and so KK is homothetic to K∩(K+x)K\cap(K+x). By Lemma 2.3, KK is a simplex.

Second, assume that (b) holds and take x∈int⁡(tK−(st−1)​tK)x\in\inter\big(tK-(st^{-1})tK\big). Then (t​K−x)∩s​K(tK-x)\cap sK is homothetic to KK. Equivalently, (t​K)∩(s​K+x)=(t​K)∩((s​t−1)​t​K+x)(tK)\cap(sK+x)=(tK)\cap\big((st^{-1})tK+x\big) is homothetic to t​KtK. Since dim(t​K)=n\dim(tK)=n and s​t−1∈(0,1]st^{-1}\in(0,1], Lemma 2.3 implies that KK is a simplex. ∎

It is well known (and easy to verify) that if K=SnK=S_{n} is an nn-simplex, all these properties hold. We will need an explicit description of the intersection from Corollary 2.4(a) in this case. Choose affine functions Aj:ℝn→ℝA_{j}\colon\mathbb{R}^{n}\to\mathbb{R}, j=0,…,nj=0,\dots,n, as above and write Aj​(x)=αj​(x)+βjA_{j}(x)=\alpha_{j}(x)+\beta_{j}, where αj:ℝn→ℝ\alpha_{j}\colon\mathbb{R}^{n}\to\mathbb{R} is linear and βj∈ℝ\beta_{j}\in\mathbb{R}. Then for 𝒘=(w1,…,wp)∈ℝn​p\bm{w}=(w_{1},\dots,w_{p})\in\mathbb{R}^{np} we have

Sn−wi={x∈ℝn:Aj(x)≥−αj(wi),j=0,…,n},i=1,…,p.S_{n}-w_{i}=\{x\in\mathbb{R}^{n}\,:\,A_{j}(x)\geq-\alpha_{j}(w_{i}),j=0,\dots,n\},\quad i=1,\dots,p.

Thus

Sn∩⋂i=1p(Sn−wi)={x∈ℝn:Aj(x)≥mj(𝒘),j=0,…,n},S_{n}\cap\bigcap_{i=1}^{p}(S_{n}-w_{i})=\{x\in\mathbb{R}^{n}\,:\,A_{j}(x)\geq m_{j}(\bm{w}),j=0,\dots,n\},

where mj​(𝒘):=max⁡{0,−αj​(w1),…,−αj​(wp)}m_{j}(\bm{w}):=\max\{0,-\alpha_{j}(w_{1}),\dots,-\alpha_{j}(w_{p})\}, j=0,…,nj=0,\dots,n. Put

(10) ρ⁡(𝒘):=1−∑j=0nmj​(𝒘)andy⁡(𝒘):=∑j=0nmj​(𝒘)​vj.\displaystyle\rho(\bm{w}):=1-\sum_{j=0}^{n}m_{j}(\bm{w})\qquad\text{and}\qquad y(\bm{w}):=\sum_{j=0}^{n}m_{j}(\bm{w})v_{j}.

Then a straightforward calculation shows that

(11) Sn∩⋂i=1p(Sn−wi)={y⁡(𝒘)+ρ⁡(𝒘)​Sn,if ​ρ​(𝒘)≥0;∅,if ​ρ​(𝒘)<0.\displaystyle S_{n}\cap\bigcap_{i=1}^{p}(S_{n}-w_{i})=\begin{cases}y(\bm{w})+\rho(\bm{w})S_{n},&\text{if }\rho(\bm{w})\geq 0;\\ \emptyset,&\text{if }\rho(\bm{w})<0.\end{cases}

Observe also that for s>0s>0 one has ρ⁡(s​𝒘)=1−s⁡(1−ρ⁡(𝒘))\rho(s\bm{w})=1-s\big(1-\rho(\bm{w})\big) and y⁡(s​𝒘)=s​y​(𝒘)y(s\bm{w})=sy(\bm{w}).

2.4. Minkowski asymmetry measure

Let K∈𝒦⁡(ℝn)K\in\mathcal{K}(\mathbb{R}^{n}) be a convex body with dimK=n\dim K=n. The Minkowski asymmetry measure of KK is defined by

s⁡(K)≔inf{t>0:−K⊂x+t​K​ for some ​x∈ℝn},s(K)\coloneqq\inf\Big\{t>0\,:\,-K\subset x+tK\text{ for some }x\in\mathbb{R}^{n}\Big\},

see [6, §6.1]. It holds s⁡(K)∈[1,n]s(K)\in[1,n] and there always exists x∈ℝnx\in\mathbb{R}^{n} such that

−K⊂x+s⁡(K)​K.-K\subset x+s(K)K.

Observe that s⁡(−K)=s⁡(K)s(-K)=s(K). Moreover, we have s⁡(K)=1s(K)=1 if and only if KK is symmetric and s⁡(K)=ns(K)=n if and only if KK is a simplex. Finally, the map

s:{K∈𝒦⁡(ℝn):dim(K)=n}→[1,n]s\colon\{K\in\mathcal{K}(\mathbb{R}^{n})\,:\,\dim(K)=n\}\to[1,n]

is continuous in the Hausdorff metric. Observe that these properties together with the monotonicity of mixed volume imply at once the cases j=1,n−1j=1,n-1 of Conjecture 1.1.

2.5. Mixed volumes

The mixed volume of convex bodies K1,…,Kn∈𝒦⁡(ℝn)K_{1},\dots,K_{n}\in\mathcal{K}(\mathbb{R}^{n}) is defined as

V⁡(K1,…,Kn)≔1n!​∂n∂t1⋯∂tn|t1=⋯=tn=0​|t1​K1+⋯+tn​Kn|.V(K_{1},\dots,K_{n})\coloneqq\frac{1}{n!}\left.\frac{\partial^{n}}{\partial t_{1}\cdots\partial t_{n}}\right|_{t_{1}=\cdots=t_{n}=0}|t_{1}K_{1}+\dots+t_{n}K_{n}|.

According to a classical result of Minkowski, the function (t1,…,tn)↦|t1​K1+⋯+tn​Kn|(t_{1},\dots,t_{n})\mapsto|t_{1}K_{1}+\dots+t_{n}K_{n}| is, in fact, an nn-homogeneous polynomial on ℝ+n\mathbb{R}_{+}^{n}.

Mixed volumes satisfy the following identities that will be used throughout the paper. Let L,K1,…,Kn∈𝒦⁡(ℝn)L,K_{1},\dots,K_{n}\in\mathcal{K}(\mathbb{R}^{n}) be convex bodies, a≥0a\geq 0, ρ:{1,…,n}→{1,…,n}\rho\colon\{1,\dots,n\}\to\{1,\dots,n\} a permutation, and T:ℝn→ℝnT\colon\mathbb{R}^{n}\to\mathbb{R}^{n} a linear endomorphism. Then

V⁡(K1+α​L,…,Kn)\displaystyle V(K_{1}+\alpha L,\dots,K_{n}) =V⁡(K1,…,Kn)+α​V​(L,K2,…,Kn),\displaystyle=V(K_{1},\dots,K_{n})+\alpha V(L,K_{2},\dots,K_{n}),
V⁡(L,L,…,L)\displaystyle V(L,L,\dots,L) =|L|,\displaystyle=|L|,
V⁡(Kρ⁡(1),…,Kρ⁡(n))\displaystyle V(K_{\rho(1)},\dots,K_{\rho(n)}) =V⁡(K1,…,Kn),\displaystyle=V(K_{1},\dots,K_{n}),
V⁡(T⁡(K1),…,T⁡(Kn))\displaystyle V\big(T(K_{1}),\dots,T(K_{n})\big) =|det(T)|​V​(K1,…,Kn)\displaystyle=|\det(T)|V(K_{1},\dots,K_{n})

If L⊂K1L\subset K_{1}, then

V⁡(L,K2,…,Kn)≤V⁡(K1,K2,…,Kn);V(L,K_{2},\dots,K_{n})\leq V(K_{1},K_{2},\dots,K_{n});

in particular,

V⁡(K1,…,Kn)≥0.V(K_{1},\dots,K_{n})\geq 0.

Moreover, V⁡(K1,…,Kn)>0V(K_{1},\dots,K_{n})>0 if and only if there exist segments Ii⊂KiI_{i}\subset K_{i}, i=1,…,ni=1,\dots,n, with linearly independent directions.

Let us emphasize that throughout the article the Lebesgue measure and the mixed volume will be considered on Euclidean spaces of various dimensions. We believe it should always be clear from the context what the dimension is.

3. Higher-order Godbersen conjectures in low dimensions

We will first verify Conjectures 1.2 and 1.3 for certain extremal values of parameters jj and j0,…,jpj_{0},\dots,j_{p}, respectively. As we will see, such special cases in particular imply that the conjectures are true in low dimensions.

Let p∈ℕp\in\mathbb{N}. Recall that ιi:ℝn→ℝp​n\iota_{i}:\mathbb{R}^{n}\to\mathbb{R}^{pn}, 1≤i≤p1\leq i\leq p, denotes the inclusion into the ii-th factor of ℝp​n=ℝn×⋯ℝn\mathbb{R}^{pn}=\mathbb{R}^{n}\times\cdots\mathbb{R}^{n}, i.e., ιi​(x)=(0,…,0,x,0,…,0)\iota_{i}(x)=(0,\dots,0,x,0,\dots,0) for x∈ℝnx\in\mathbb{R}^{n}. Moreover, the following notation will be used for the rest of the paper: We set

𝒥pn:={(j0,…,jp)∈ℕ0p+1:j0+⋯+jp=n},\mathcal{J}_{p}^{n}:=\left\{(j_{0},\dots,j_{p})\in\mathbb{N}^{p+1}_{0}\,:\,j_{0}+\cdots+j_{p}=n\right\},

and for a fixed K∈𝒦⁡(ℝn)K\in\mathcal{K}(\mathbb{R}^{n}) we define the function Wp,K:𝒥pn→ℝ+W_{p,K}:\mathcal{J}_{p}^{n}\to\mathbb{R}_{+} by

Wp,K​(𝒋):=V⁡(−Δp​K​[n−j0],ι1​K​[n−j1],…,ιp​K​[n−jp]),𝒋=(j0,…,jp)∈𝒥pn.W_{p,K}(\bm{j}):=V\big(-\Delta_{p}K[n-j_{0}],\iota_{1}K[n-j_{1}],\dots,\iota_{p}K[n-j_{p}]\big),\quad\bm{j}=(j_{0},\dots,j_{p})\in\mathcal{J}_{p}^{n}.

For 𝒋=(j0,…,jp)∈𝒥pn\bm{j}=(j_{0},\dots,j_{p})\in\mathcal{J}_{p}^{n} we will also abbreviate

(n𝒋):=(nj0,…,jp)and(n​pn−𝒋):=(n​pn−j0,…,n−jp).{n\choose\bm{j}}:={n\choose j_{0},\dots,j_{p}}\qquad\text{and}\qquad{np\choose n-\bm{j}}:={np\choose n-j_{0},\dots,n-j_{p}}.

We will repeatedly use the following simple observation:

Lemma 3.1 ([11, Remarks 3.4 and 3.5]).

For each p≥2p\geq 2 and K∈𝒦⁡(ℝn)K\in\mathcal{K}(\mathbb{R}^{n}), the function Wp,KW_{p,K} is symmetric and satisfies

Wp,K​(j0,…,jp−1,0)=(n​pn)−1​|K|​Wp−1,K​(j0,…,jp−1),(j0,…,jp−1)∈𝒥p−1n.\displaystyle W_{p,\,K}(j_{0},\dots,j_{p-1},0)={np\choose n}^{-1}|K|\,W_{p-1,\,K}(j_{0},\dots,j_{p-1}),\quad(j_{0},\dots,j_{p-1})\in\mathcal{J}_{p-1}^{n}.

When studying Conjecture 1.3, we may thus assume ji>0j_{i}>0 for i=0,…,pi=0,\dots,p and, in particular, p≤n−1p\leq n-1. The case p=n−1p=n-1 of the inequality (5) is due to Janson which was mentioned without proof by Schneider [24, p. 537]; we include an argument here for completeness.

Proposition 3.2 (Janson’s inequality).

For any K∈𝒦⁡(ℝn)K\in\mathcal{K}(\mathbb{R}^{n}) we have

(12) Wn−1,K​(1,…,1)≤(n!)n(n2−n)!​|K|n−1.W_{n-1,K}(1,\dots,1)\leq\frac{(n!)^{n}}{(n^{2}-n)!}|K|^{n-1}.
Proof.

For any q∈ℕq\in\mathbb{N}, Schneider’s inequality (3) yields

∑𝒋∈𝒥qn(n​qn−𝒋)​Wq,K​(𝒋)≤(n​q+nn)​|K|q.\sum_{\bm{j}\in\mathcal{J}_{q}^{n}}{nq\choose n-\bm{j}}W_{q,K}(\bm{j})\leq{nq+n\choose n}|K|^{q}.

Assume q≥n−1q\geq n-1 and consider only the summands corresponding to 𝒋∈𝒥qn∩{0,1}q+1\bm{j}\in\mathcal{J}_{q}^{n}\cap\{0,1\}^{q+1}, i.e., to the multiindices with entries 0 and 1. By Lemma 3.1, for each such term we have

(n​qn−𝒋)​Wq,K​(1,…,1,0,…,0)=(n⁡(n−1)n−1,…,n−1)​|K|q+1−n​Wn−1,K​(1,…,1).{nq\choose n-\bm{j}}W_{q,K}(1,\dots,1,0,\dots,0)={n(n-1)\choose n-1,\dots,n-1}|K|^{q+1-n}W_{n-1,K}(1,\dots,1).

Using this and restricting the above sum to (q+1n){q+1\choose n} such summands, we get

(q+1n)​(n⁡(n−1)n−1,…,n−1)​|K|q+1−n​Wn−1,K​(1,…,1)≤(n​q+nn)​|K|q.{q+1\choose n}{n(n-1)\choose n-1,\dots,n-1}|K|^{q+1-n}W_{n-1,K}(1,\dots,1)\leq{nq+n\choose n}|K|^{q}.

Letting q→∞q\to\infty easily yields (12). ∎

Note that the limiting argument in the proof of Proposition 3.2 does not allow for analysis of equality cases of (12). In fact, we do not know if simplices are the only non-trivial extremizers in this case.

Proof of Theorem 1.4(b).

If n=2n=2 then we may assume p=1p=1 and j0=j1=1j_{0}=j_{1}=1 which is the known case j=1j=1 of Conjecture 1.1.

Let n=3n=3. The only two cases to consider correspond to the multiindices (2,1)(2,1) and (1,1,1)(1,1,1) for p=1p=1 and p=2p=2, respectively. The former is again a known case of Conjecture 1.1, the latter is a special case of Proposition 3.2. ∎

By [11, Proposition 3.3], Theorem 1.4(b) implies that the same is true for Conjecture 1.2. In what follows, we will establish additional cases of Conjecture 1.2 that in particular include the characterization of equality cases in dimension n=3n=3, thus proving Theorem 1.4(a). Namely, we will prove the conjecture for j∈{0,1,n−1,n}j\in\{0,1,n-1,n\}. Observe that, unlike in the case p=1p=1, for p≥2p\geq 2 there is in general no symmetry between the mixed volumes V⁡(Kp​[n​p−j],−Δp​K​[j])V(K^{p}[np-j],-\Delta_{p}K[j]) and V⁡(Kp​[n​p−n+j],−Δp​K​[n−j])V(K^{p}[np-n+j],-\Delta_{p}K[n-j]).

First, Conjecture 1.2 is trivial for j=0j=0. Second, assuming p≥2p\geq 2, an argument similar to [11, Remark 3.5(c)] yields at once

V⁡(Kp​[n​p−n],−Δp​K​[n])=(n​pn)−1​|K|​|Dp−1​K|,V(K^{p}[np-n],-\Delta_{p}K[n])={np\choose n}^{-1}|K|\,|D_{p-1}K|,

which together with Schneider’s inequality (3) proves the case j=nj=n. Third, writing Kp=∑i=1pιi​KK^{p}=\sum_{i=1}^{p}\iota_{i}K, expanding by multilinearity, and using Lemma 3.1, gives

V⁡(Kp​[n​p−1],−Δp​K)=|K|p−1​V​(K⁡[n−1],−K).V(K^{p}[np-1],-\Delta_{p}K)=|K|^{p-1}V(K[n-1],-K).

Hence, if j=1j=1, Conjecture 1.2 is for general p∈ℕp\in\mathbb{N} equivalent to the known case p=1p=1. Finally, since no closed formula for the mixed volume V⁡(Kp​[n​p−n+1],−Δp​K​[n−1])V(K^{p}[np-n+1],-\Delta_{p}K[n-1]) is known to us, we will deduce the case j=n−1j=n-1 from the following general statement which might be of independent interest:

Proposition 3.3.

Let p∈ℕp\in\mathbb{N} and 0≤j≤n0\leq j\leq n. For any K,L∈𝒦⁡(ℝn)K,L\in\mathcal{K}(\mathbb{R}^{n}) one has

(n​pj)​V​(Kp​[n​p−j],−Δp​L​[j])=(nj)​∫Dp−1​KV⁡(K𝒘​[n−j],−L⁡[j])​d​𝒘,{np\choose j}V(K^{p}[np-j],-\Delta_{p}L[j])={n\choose j}\int\limits_{D_{p-1}K}V(K_{\bm{w}}[n-j],-L[j])\,\textup{d}\bm{w},

where

K𝒘:=K∩⋂i=1p−1(K−wi),𝒘=(w1,…,wp−1)∈(ℝn)p−1.K_{\bm{w}}:=K\cap\bigcap_{i=1}^{p-1}(K-w_{i}),\quad\bm{w}=(w_{1},\dots,w_{p-1})\in(\mathbb{R}^{n})^{p-1}.

Consider the linear map F:ℝn​p→ℝn​pF\colon\mathbb{R}^{np}\to\mathbb{R}^{np} given by

F⁡(x1,…,xp)≔(x1−xp,…,xp−1−xp,xp).F(x_{1},\dots,x_{p})\coloneqq(x_{1}-x_{p},\dots,x_{p-1}-x_{p},x_{p}).

F⁡(Kp−t​Δp​L)={(𝒘,z)∈ℝn​p−n×ℝn:z∈K𝒘−t​L}F(K^{p}-t\Delta_{p}L)=\big\{(\bm{w},z)\in\mathbb{R}^{np-n}\times\mathbb{R}^{n}\,:\,z\in K_{\bm{w}}-tL\big\}

for any t>0t>0. Consequently, Fubini’s theorem yields

=|F⁡(Kp−t​Δp​L)|\displaystyle=\left|F(K^{p}-t\Delta_{p}L)\right|
=∫ℝn​p−n|K𝒘−t​L|​d​𝒘\displaystyle=\int\limits_{\mathbb{R}^{np-n}}|K_{\bm{w}}-tL|\,\textup{d}\bm{w}
=∑j=0n(nj)​tj​∫Dp−1​KV⁡(K𝒘​[n−j],−L⁡[j])​d​𝒘,\displaystyle=\sum_{j=0}^{n}{n\choose j}t^{j}\int\limits_{D_{p-1}K}V(K_{\bm{w}}[n-j],-L[j])\,\textup{d}\bm{w},

where we used the fact that K𝒘≠∅K_{\bm{w}}\neq\emptyset if and only if 𝒘∈Dp−1​K.\bm{w}\in D_{p-1}K. Comparing the coefficients of tjt^{j}, the claim follows. ∎

The integral formula of Proposition 3.3 gives for general jj a (weaker) upper bound than (4) which, however, does not depend on pp:

Proposition 3.4.

In particular, s⁡(K𝒘)<ns(K_{\bm{w}})<n and V⁡(K𝒘,K⁡[n−1])>0V(K_{\bm{w}},K[n-1])>0 on a subset of Dp−1​KD_{p-1}K of positive (n​p−n)(np-n)-dimensional measure, which makes the second inequality in the proof of Proposition 3.4 strict and completes the proof. ∎

Proof of Theorem 1.4(a).

If n∈{2,3}n\in\{2,3\}, then necessarily j∈{0,1,n−1,n}j\in\{0,1,n-1,n\}. We have seen that Conjecture 1.2 is true in these cases. ∎

4. Higher-order Godbersen conjectures for special classes of convex bodies

In this section we will use an argument due to Godbersen [5] to show that Conjectures 1.2 and 1.3 hold for convex bodies of constant width if n≤6n\leq 6, in the latter case for n=6n=6 possibly without the characterization of equality cases. Along the way, we will also observe that in general dimension the conjectures hold for symmetric convex bodies; note that although this is rather easy to see, it is not as obvious as in the classical case p=1p=1.

Recall from [5] that if K∈𝒦⁡(ℝn)K\in\mathcal{K}(\mathbb{R}^{n}) is of constant width, then there exists x∈ℝnx\in\mathbb{R}^{n} such that

−K⊂x+αn​K,-K\subset x+\alpha_{n}K,

where

αn:=n+2​n​(n+1)n+2.\alpha_{n}:=\frac{n+\sqrt{2n(n+1)}}{n+2}.

Observe that in particular s⁡(K)≤αns(K)\leq\alpha_{n}. Moreover, this constant is optimal in the sense that there exists K~∈𝒦⁡(ℝn)\widetilde{K}\in\mathcal{K}(\mathbb{R}^{n}) of constant width for which s⁡(K~)=αn.s(\widetilde{K})=\alpha_{n}. Godbersen’s proof of Conjecture 1.1 for bodies of constant width is based on following estimate:

Lemma 4.1 ([5, §7]).

For any 1≤j≤⌊n2⌋1\leq j\leq\lfloor\frac{n}{2}\rfloor it holds that

(αn)j<(nj).(\alpha_{n})^{j}<{n\choose j}.
Proof of Theorem 1.4(c).

Observe that for any K∈𝒦⁡(ℝn)K\in\mathcal{K}(\mathbb{R}^{n}) we have

V⁡(−Δp​K​[j],Kp​[n​p−j])≤s​(K)j​|K|p.V\big(-\Delta_{p}K[j],K^{p}[np-j]\big)\leq s(K)^{j}|K|^{p}.

Hence, the statement for j≤⌊n2⌋j\leq\lfloor\frac{n}{2}\rfloor follows at once from Lemma 4.1 and the fact that s⁡(K)≤αns(K)\leq\alpha_{n} for bodies of constant width. Proceeding to the case n≤6n\leq 6, by the results of Section 3 we may assume 2≤j≤n−22\leq j\leq n-2 and n∈{4,5,6}n\in\{4,5,6\}. A short calculation shows that the desired inequalities

s(K)j<(nj),j=2,…,n−2,s(K)^{j}<{n\choose j},\qquad j=2,\dots,n-2,

hold if and only if

s⁡(K)<βn≔(nn−2)1n−2.s(K)<\beta_{n}\coloneqq{n\choose n-2}^{\frac{1}{n-2}}.

Using s⁡(K)≤αns(K)\leq\alpha_{n}, it suffices to verify that αn<βn\alpha_{n}<\beta_{n} for n∈{4,5,6}n\in\{4,5,6\}. To this end, we compute

α4=2+103≈1.721\displaystyle\alpha_{4}=\frac{2+\sqrt{10}}{3}\approx 1.721 <2.449≈6=β4\displaystyle<2.449\approx\sqrt{6}=\beta_{4}
α5=5+2​157≈1.821\displaystyle\alpha_{5}=\frac{5+2\sqrt{15}}{7}\approx 1.821 <2.154≈1013=β5\displaystyle<2.154\approx 10^{\frac{1}{3}}=\beta_{5}
α6=3+214≈1.896\displaystyle\alpha_{6}=\frac{3+\sqrt{21}}{4}\approx 1.896 <1.968≈1514=β6.\displaystyle<1.968\approx 15^{\frac{1}{4}}=\beta_{6}.

∎

Observe that in higher dimensions this method fails as

αn≥α7=7+4​79≈1.953>1.838≈2115=β7≥βn,n≥7.\alpha_{n}\geq\alpha_{7}=\frac{7+4\sqrt{7}}{9}\approx 1.953>1.838\approx 21^{\frac{1}{5}}=\beta_{7}\geq\beta_{n},\qquad n\geq 7.

We will now apply an analogous argument to the finer coefficients in Conjecture 1.3.

Let p∈ℕp\in\mathbb{N} and consider a full-dimensional convex body K∈𝒦⁡(ℝn)K\in\mathcal{K}(\mathbb{R}^{n}). To prove (5) for n∈{4,5,6}n\in\{4,5,6\}, it remains to consider 𝒋∈𝒥pn\bm{j}\in\mathcal{J}_{p}^{n} with 1≤j0,…,jp≤n−21\leq j_{0},\dots,j_{p}\leq n-2. Then, using the symmetry of Wp,KW_{p,K}, we may assume that j0≥2j_{0}\geq 2 and hence the computations from the proof of Theorem 1.4(c) imply

5. Stability of the higher-order Godbersen conjectures under products

In this section we will show that Conjectures 1.2 and 1.3 are stable under the operation of taking Cartesian products. More precisely, we will prove that if Ki∈𝒦⁡(ℝni)K_{i}\in\mathcal{K}(\mathbb{R}^{n_{i}}), i=1,2i=1,2, satisfy Conjecture 1.3 for p∈ℕp\in\mathbb{N}, then K1×K2∈𝒦⁡(ℝn1+n2)K_{1}\times K_{2}\in\mathcal{K}(\mathbb{R}^{n_{1}+n_{2}}) satisfies Conjecture 1.3 for this value of pp. The proof of the corresponding statement for Conjecture 1.2 is analogous (and simpler) and so we omit it.

Throughout this section, we will denote n:=n1+n2n:=n_{1}+n_{2} and, for simplicity, we will interchangeably regard the space ℝp​n\mathbb{R}^{pn} both as (ℝn1×ℝn2)p(\mathbb{R}^{n_{1}}\times\mathbb{R}^{n_{2}})^{p} and (ℝn1)p×(ℝn2)p(\mathbb{R}^{n_{1}})^{p}\times(\mathbb{R}^{n_{2}})^{p}. Moreover, for any 𝒋∈𝒥pn\bm{j}\in\mathcal{J}_{p}^{n} we will denote

ℐ⁡(𝒋):={(𝒋1,𝒋2)∈𝒥pn1×𝒥pn2:𝒋1+𝒋2=𝒋}.\mathcal{I}(\bm{j}):=\left\{(\bm{j}^{1},\bm{j}^{2})\in\mathcal{J}^{n_{1}}_{p}\times\mathcal{J}^{n_{2}}_{p}\,:\,\bm{j}^{1}+\bm{j}^{2}=\bm{j}\right\}.

We will first show that the higher-order difference body and its mixed-volume coefficients behave naturally under products.

Lemma 5.1.

Let p∈ℕp\in\mathbb{N}. For any K1∈𝒦⁡(ℝn1)K_{1}\in\mathcal{K}(\mathbb{R}^{n_{1}}) and K2∈𝒦⁡(ℝn2)K_{2}\in\mathcal{K}(\mathbb{R}^{n_{2}}) one has

(14) Dp​(K1×K2)=Dp​K1×Dp​K2.\displaystyle D_{p}(K_{1}\times K_{2})=D_{p}K_{1}\times D_{p}K_{2}.

Moreover, for any 𝐣∈𝒥pn\bm{j}\in\mathcal{J}^{n}_{p}, one has

(15) (n​pn−𝒋)​Wp,K1×K2​(𝒋)=∑(𝒋1,𝒋2)∈ℐ⁡(𝒋)(n1​pn1−𝒋1)​(n2​pn2−𝒋2)​Wp,K1​(𝒋1)​Wp,K2​(𝒋2).\displaystyle{np\choose n-\bm{j}}\,W_{p,K_{1}\times K_{2}}(\bm{j})=\sum\limits_{(\bm{j}^{1},\,\bm{j}^{2})\in\mathcal{I}(\bm{j})}{n_{1}p\choose n_{1}-\bm{j}^{1}}{n_{2}p\choose n_{2}-\bm{j}^{2}}\,W_{p,K_{1}}(\bm{j}^{1})W_{p,K_{2}}(\bm{j}^{2}).

Denote K:=K1×K2K:=K_{1}\times K_{2}. With the above identification, we have Δp​K=Δp​K1×Δp​K2\Delta_{p}K=\Delta_{p}K_{1}\times\Delta_{p}K_{2} and ιi​K=ιi​K1×ιi​K2\iota_{i}K=\iota_{i}K_{1}\times\iota_{i}K_{2}, i=1,…,pi=1,\dots,p. Hence for any μ1,…,μp>0\mu_{1},\dots,\mu_{p}>0, we get

−Δp​K+∑l=1pμl​ιl​K=(−Δp​K1+∑l=1pμl​ιl​K1)×(−Δp​K2+∑l=1pμl​ιl​K2).\displaystyle-\Delta_{p}K+\sum_{l=1}^{p}\mu_{l}\iota_{l}K=\left(-\Delta_{p}K_{1}+\sum_{l=1}^{p}\mu_{l}\iota_{l}K_{1}\right)\times\left(-\Delta_{p}K_{2}+\sum_{l=1}^{p}\mu_{l}\iota_{l}K_{2}\right).

Putting μ1=⋯=μp=1\mu_{1}=\cdots=\mu_{p}=1 proves (14). On the other hand, taking the volume and polarizing easily yields (15). ∎

The following observation will later be used to estimate the sum in (15).

Lemma 5.2.

Let p∈ℕp\in\mathbb{N}. For any 𝐣∈𝒥pn\bm{j}\in\mathcal{J}_{p}^{n} satisfying j0,…,jp<nj_{0},\dots,j_{p}<n we have

Using the usual convention (ab):=0{a\choose b}:=0 for b>ab>a, we have

≥∑(𝒋1,𝒋2)∈ℐ⁡(𝒋)∏l=0p(n1jl1)​∏k=0p(n2jk2).\displaystyle\geq\sum\limits_{(\bm{j}^{1},\,\bm{j}^{2})\in\mathcal{I}(\bm{j})}\prod_{l=0}^{p}{n_{1}\choose j_{l}^{1}}\prod_{k=0}^{p}{n_{2}\choose j_{k}^{2}}.

We will prove that the last inequality is in fact strict by showing that the penultimate sum contains at least one positive summand that is omitted in the last sum. For each l∈{0,…,p}l\in\{0,\dots,p\}, the values of jl1j_{l}^{1} for which the corresponding summand is positive are exactly the integers from

ℕ0∩[max⁡{0,jl−n2},min⁡{n1,jl}].\mathbb{N}_{0}\cap\left[\max\{0,j_{l}-n_{2}\},\min\{n_{1},j_{l}\}\right].

Since j0,…,jp<nj_{0},\dots,j_{p}<n, there exists an index jl0j_{l_{0}} with 1≤jl0≤n−11\leq j_{l_{0}}\leq n-1 and hence the number of such integers is at least two in this case. We can now proceed to the proof of the stability of Conjecture 1.3 under Cartesian products.

6. Higher-order difference body and weighted inequalities for −Δp​K-\Delta_{p}K and KpK^{p}

In this section we deal with two consequences of Conjecture 1.2, namely, sharp inequalities for two different weighted sums of the mixed volumes of −Δp​K-\Delta_{p}K and KpK^{p}, see Theorems 1.5 and 1.7. The former is proven here, the latter will be deduced in the next section as a consequence of a more general statement. We also consider here a higher-order generalization of the unbalanced difference body and show that the corresponding weighted Schneider–Rogers–Shephard type inequality (Conjecture 1.8), which is weaker than Conjecture 1.2, would still imply both Theorems 1.5 and 1.7.

The following notation will be used throughout the entire section: For p∈ℕp\in\mathbb{N}, t∈[0,1]t\in[0,1], and K∈𝒦⁡(ℝn)K\in\mathcal{K}(\mathbb{R}^{n}) we define

Equivalently, one has

Cp,t,K={(s,(1−s)(1−t)y−stΔp(x)):s∈[0,1],x∈K,y∈Kp}.C_{p,t,K}=\left\{\big(s,(1-s)(1-t)y-st\Delta_{p}(x)\big)\,:\,s\in[0,1],\,x\in K,\,y\in K^{p}\right\}.

We will also repeatedly use the following well-known integral formula for k,l∈ℕ0k,l\in\mathbb{N}_{0}:

∎

(21) |Dpt​Sn|=(1−t)n⁡(p−1)​∑j=0n(n​pj)​(nj)​(1−t)n−j​tj​|Sn|p.|D_{p}^{t}S_{n}|=(1-t)^{n(p-1)}\sum_{j=0}^{n}{np\choose j}{n\choose j}(1-t)^{n-j}t^{j}|S_{n}|^{p}.

∑j=0n(n​pj)​(1−t)n−j​tj​V​(Kp​[n​p−j],−Δp​K​[j])≤∑j=0n(n​pj)​(nj)​(1−t)n−j​tj​|K|p,t∈[0,1].\sum_{j=0}^{n}{np\choose j}(1-t)^{n-j}t^{j}V(K^{p}[np-j],-\Delta_{p}K[j])\leq\sum_{j=0}^{n}{np\choose j}{n\choose j}(1-t)^{n-j}t^{j}|K|^{p},\quad t\in[0,1].

7. Higher-order difference body and weighted inequalities for −Δp​K-\Delta_{p}K and ι1​K,…,ιp​K\iota_{1}K,\dots,\iota_{p}K

Now we will generalize the results of Artstein-Avidan and Putterman [2] to the context of Conjecture 1.3. First, we will prove two consequences of the conjecture, namely, sharp inequalities for two different weighted sums of the mixed volumes of −Δp​K-\Delta_{p}K and ι1​K,…,ιp​K\iota_{1}K,\dots,\iota_{p}K, and deduce Theorem 1.7 from one of them. Second, we will define the corresponding higher-order unbalanced difference body and show that phenomena analogous to those proven in the previous section persist in the context of Conjecture 1.3. Namely, we will conjecture the corresponding weighted Schneider–Rogers–Shephard type inequality, weaker than Conjecture 1.3, and we will show that it still implies the weighted inequalities.

Let us establish a notation that will be used throughout the entire section. Fix p∈ℕp\in\mathbb{N}. First, we will keep the notation 𝒥pn\mathcal{J}_{p}^{n}, Wp,KW_{p,K}, (n𝒋){n\choose\bm{j}}, and (n​pn−𝒋){np\choose n-\bm{j}} from Section 3. Further, we will consider the standard pp-simplex in ℝp+1\mathbb{R}^{p+1} given by

Θp:={(t0,…,tp)∈ℝ+p+1:t0+⋯+tp=1}\Theta_{p}:=\left\{(t_{0},\dots,t_{p})\in\mathbb{R}^{p+1}_{+}\,:\,t_{0}+\cdots+t_{p}=1\right\}

and for 𝒕=(t0,…,tp)∈Θp\bm{t}=(t_{0},\dots,t_{p})\in\Theta_{p} we will denote

𝒕^:=(t1,…,tp)andΘ^p:={𝒕^:𝒕∈Θp}.\hat{\bm{t}}:=(t_{1},\dots,t_{p})\qquad\text{and}\qquad\hat{\Theta}_{p}:=\{\hat{\bm{t}}\,:\,\bm{t}\in\Theta_{p}\}.

Observe that the map Θp→Θ^p:𝒕↦𝒕^\Theta_{p}\to\hat{\Theta}_{p}:\bm{t}\mapsto\hat{\bm{t}} is a bijection. When 𝒋=(j0,…,jp)∈𝒥pn\bm{j}=(j_{0},\dots,j_{p})\in\mathcal{J}_{p}^{n}, k∈ℕ0k\in\mathbb{N}_{0}, and 𝒌=(k0,…,kp)∈(ℕ0)p+1\bm{k}=(k_{0},\dots,k_{p})\in(\mathbb{N}_{0})^{p+1}, we will also abbreviate

𝒕n−𝒋:=∏l=0ptln−jl,𝒕k:=∏l=0ptlk,and𝒕𝒌:=∏l=0ptlkl.\bm{t}^{n-\bm{j}}:=\prod_{l=0}^{p}t_{l}^{n-j_{l}},\qquad\bm{t}^{k}:=\prod_{l=0}^{p}t_{l}^{k},\qquad\text{and}\qquad\bm{t}^{\bm{k}}:=\prod_{l=0}^{p}t_{l}^{k_{l}}.

Let e1,…,epe_{1},\dots,e_{p} be the standard basis of ℝp\mathbb{R}^{p}. For any K∈𝒦⁡(ℝn)K\in\mathcal{K}(\mathbb{R}^{n}) and 𝒕∈Θp\bm{t}\in\Theta_{p} we define

(23) Gp,𝒕,K:=({0}×−t0ΔpK)∨⋁l=1p({el}×tlιlK)∈𝒦(ℝp×ℝp​n).\displaystyle G_{p,\bm{t},K}:=(\{0\}\times-t_{0}\Delta_{p}K)\vee\bigvee_{l=1}^{p}(\{e_{l}\}\times t_{l}\iota_{l}K)\in\mathcal{K}(\mathbb{R}^{p}\times\mathbb{R}^{pn}).

Equivalently,

Gp,𝒕,K={(𝒔^,−s0t0Δp(x0)+s1t1ι1(x1)+⋯+sptpιp(xp)):x0,…,xp∈K,𝒔∈Θp}.G_{p,\bm{t},K}=\left\{\big(\hat{\bm{s}},-s_{0}t_{0}\Delta_{p}(x_{0})+s_{1}t_{1}\iota_{1}(x_{1})+\dots+s_{p}t_{p}\iota_{p}(x_{p})\big)\,:\,x_{0},\dots,x_{p}\in K,\bm{s}\in\Theta_{p}\right\}.

We will also repeatedly use the following formula which is a direct generalization of (17):

(24) ∫Θ^p𝒔𝒌​d​𝒔^=k0!⋯kp!(k0+⋯+kp+p)!,𝒌∈(ℕ0)p+1.\displaystyle\int_{\hat{\Theta}_{p}}\bm{s}^{\bm{k}}\,\textup{d}\hat{\bm{s}}=\frac{k_{0}!\cdots k_{p}!}{(k_{0}+\cdots+k_{p}+p)!},\quad\bm{k}\in(\mathbb{N}_{0})^{p+1}.

7.1. Weighted inequalities II

Lemma 7.1.

Let p∈ℕp\in\mathbb{N}. For any K∈𝒦⁡(ℝn)K\in\mathcal{K}(\mathbb{R}^{n}) and 𝐭∈Θp\bm{t}\in\Theta_{p} we have

(25) |Gp,𝒕,K|=(n​p)!(n​p+p)!​∑𝒋∈𝒥pn𝒕n−𝒋​Wp,K​(𝒋).\displaystyle|G_{p,\bm{t},K}|=\frac{(np)!}{(np+p)!}\sum_{\bm{j}\in\mathcal{J}^{n}_{p}}\bm{t}^{n-\bm{j}}W_{p,K}(\bm{j}).
Proof.

A direct computation shows

|Gp,𝒕,K|\displaystyle|G_{p,\bm{t},K}| =∫Θ^p|−s0​t0​Δp​K+∑l=1psl​tl​ιl​K|​d​𝒔^\displaystyle=\int_{\hat{\Theta}_{p}}\left|-s_{0}t_{0}\Delta_{p}K+\sum_{l=1}^{p}s_{l}t_{l}\iota_{l}K\right|\,\textup{d}\hat{\bm{s}}
=∑𝒋∈𝒥pn(n​pn−𝒋)​𝒕n−𝒋​Wp,K​(𝒋)​∫Θ^p𝒔n−𝒋​d​𝒔^\displaystyle=\sum_{\bm{j}\in\mathcal{J}^{n}_{p}}{np\choose n-\bm{j}}\bm{t}^{n-\bm{j}}W_{p,K}(\bm{j})\int_{\hat{\Theta}_{p}}\bm{s}^{n-\bm{j}}\,\textup{d}\hat{\bm{s}}
=(n​p)!(n​p+p)!​∑𝒋∈𝒥pn𝒕n−𝒋​Wp,K​(𝒋).\displaystyle=\frac{(np)!}{(np+p)!}\sum_{\bm{j}\in\mathcal{J}^{n}_{p}}\bm{t}^{n-\bm{j}}W_{p,K}(\bm{j}).

∎

Lemma 7.2.

Let p∈ℕp\in\mathbb{N}. For any K∈𝒦⁡(ℝn)K\in\mathcal{K}(\mathbb{R}^{n}) and 𝐭∈Θp\bm{t}\in\Theta_{p} we have

(26) |Gp,𝒕,K|≤(n!)p(n​p+p)!​∑𝒋∈𝒥pn(n𝒋)​𝒕n−𝒋​|K|p.\displaystyle|G_{p,\bm{t},K}|\leq\frac{(n!)^{p}}{(np+p)!}\sum_{\bm{j}\in\mathcal{J}^{n}_{p}}{n\choose\bm{j}}\bm{t}^{n-\bm{j}}|K|^{p}.
Proof.

We may assume 𝒕∈relint⁡(Θp)\bm{t}\in\relint(\Theta_{p}), the general case follows by continuity. Set

Hp,𝒕,K:={(0,t0​x0,−t0​Δp​(x0)):x∈K}∨⋁l=1p{(el,0,tl​ιl​(xl)):xl∈K}∈𝒦⁡(ℝp×ℝn×ℝn​p).\displaystyle H_{p,\bm{t},K}:=\big\{\big(0,t_{0}x_{0},-t_{0}\Delta_{p}(x_{0})\big)\,:\,x\in K\big\}\vee\bigvee_{l=1}^{p}\{\big(e_{l},0,t_{l}\iota_{l}(x_{l})\big):x_{l}\in K\}\in\mathcal{K}(\mathbb{R}^{p}\times\mathbb{R}^{n}\times\mathbb{R}^{np}).

Equivalently,

Hp,𝒕,K={(𝒔^,s0t0x0,−s0t0Δp(x0)+s1t1ι1(x1)+⋯+sptpιp(xp)):x0,…,xp∈K,𝒔∈Θp}H_{p,\bm{t},K}=\left\{\big(\hat{\bm{s}},s_{0}t_{0}x_{0},-s_{0}t_{0}\Delta_{p}(x_{0})+s_{1}t_{1}\iota_{1}(x_{1})+\cdots+s_{p}t_{p}\iota_{p}(x_{p})\big)\,:\,x_{0},\dots,x_{p}\in K,\bm{s}\in\Theta_{p}\right\}

and so we have

(27) |Hp,𝒕,K|=|K|p+1​𝒕n​∫Θ^p𝒔n​d​𝒔^=|K|p+1​(n!)p+1(n​p+n+p)!​𝒕n.\displaystyle|H_{p,\bm{t},K}|=|K|^{p+1}\bm{t}^{n}\int_{\hat{\Theta}_{p}}\bm{s}^{n}\,\textup{d}\hat{\bm{s}}=|K|^{p+1}\frac{(n!)^{p+1}}{(np+n+p)!}\bm{t}^{n}.

Next, we consider the section of Hp,𝒕,KH_{p,\bm{t},K} by the affine subspace

E𝒕:={(θ^𝒕,v,0):v∈ℝn},E_{\bm{t}}:=\{(\hat{\theta}_{\bm{t}},v,0)\,:\,v\in\mathbb{R}^{n}\},

where θ𝒕:=(∑l=0ptl−1)−1​(t0−1,…,tp−1)\theta_{\bm{t}}:=\left(\sum_{l=0}^{p}t_{l}^{-1}\right)^{-1}\left(t_{0}^{-1},\dots,t_{p}^{-1}\right), and the orthogonal projection onto E𝒕⟂E_{\bm{t}}^{\perp}. We obtain

Hp,𝒕,K∩E𝒕={(θ^𝒕,(∑l=0ptl−1)−1​x,0):x∈K}\displaystyle H_{p,\bm{t},K}\cap E_{\bm{t}}=\left\{\left(\hat{\theta}_{\bm{t}},\left(\sum_{l=0}^{p}t_{l}^{-1}\right)^{-1}x,0\right)\,:\,x\in K\right\}

and

PE𝒕⟂​(Hp,𝒕,K)\displaystyle P_{E_{\bm{t}}^{\perp}}(H_{p,\bm{t},K}) ={(𝒔^,0,y):(𝒔^,x,y)∈Hp,𝒕,K​ for some ​x∈ℝn}\displaystyle=\{(\hat{\bm{s}},0,y):(\hat{\bm{s}},x,y)\in H_{p,\bm{t},K}\text{ for some }x\in\mathbb{R}^{n}\}
={(𝒔^,0,y):y∈−s0​t0​Δp​K+s1​t1​ι1​K+⋯+sp​tp​ιp​K}\displaystyle=\{(\hat{\bm{s}},0,y):y\in-s_{0}t_{0}\Delta_{p}K+s_{1}t_{1}\iota_{1}K+\dots+s_{p}t_{p}\iota_{p}K\}
=Gp,𝒕,K.\displaystyle=G_{p,\bm{t},K}.

It follows |Hp,𝒕,K∩E𝒕|=(∑l=0ptl−1)−n​|K||H_{p,\bm{t},K}\cap E_{\bm{t}}|=\left(\sum_{l=0}^{p}t_{l}^{-1}\right)^{-n}|K| and |PE𝒕⟂​(Hp,𝒕,K)|=|Gp,𝒕,K||P_{E_{\bm{t}}^{\perp}}(H_{p,\bm{t},K})|=|G_{p,\bm{t},K}|. Applying Lemma 2.1 together with (27), we obtain

|Gp,𝒕,K|\displaystyle|G_{p,\bm{t},K}| ≤(n​p+n+pn)​|Hp,𝒕,K||K|​(∑l=0ptl−1)n=(n!)p(n​p+p)!​∑𝒋∈𝒥pn(n𝒋)​𝒕n−𝒋​|K|p,\displaystyle\leq{np+n+p\choose n}\frac{|H_{p,\bm{t},K}|}{|K|}\left(\sum_{l=0}^{p}t_{l}^{-1}\right)^{n}=\frac{(n!)^{p}}{(np+p)!}\sum_{\bm{j}\in\mathcal{J}^{n}_{p}}{n\choose\bm{j}}\bm{t}^{n-\bm{j}}|K|^{p},

which completes the proof. ∎

Theorem 7.3.

Let p∈ℕp\in\mathbb{N}. For any K∈𝒦⁡(ℝn)K\in\mathcal{K}(\mathbb{R}^{n}) and 𝐭∈Θp\bm{t}\in\Theta_{p}, one has

(28) ∑𝒋∈𝒥pn𝒕n−𝒋​Wp,K​(𝒋)≤(n!)p(n​p)!​∑𝒋∈𝒥pn(n𝒋)​𝒕n−𝒋​|K|p.\displaystyle\sum_{\bm{j}\in\mathcal{J}^{n}_{p}}\bm{t}^{n-\bm{j}}W_{p,K}(\bm{j})\leq\frac{(n!)^{p}}{(np)!}\sum_{\bm{j}\in\mathcal{J}^{n}_{p}}{n\choose\bm{j}}\bm{t}^{n-\bm{j}}|K|^{p}.

If dimK=n\dim K=n and equality holds for some 𝐭∈relint⁡(Θp)\bm{t}\in\relint(\Theta_{p}), then KK is a simplex.

Proof.

First, the inequality (28) follows at once by combining (25) with (26).

Second, assume that dim(K)=n\dim(K)=n and that equality holds in (28) for some 𝒕∈relint⁡(Θp)\bm{t}\in\relint(\Theta_{p}). Then we have equality in (26) and the proof of Lemma 7.2 together with Lemma 2.1 in turn imply that all non-empty sections of the body Hp,𝒕,KH_{p,\bm{t},K} by the affine subspaces of the form E𝒕+(0,0,𝒂)E_{\bm{t}}+(0,0,\bm{a}), where 𝒂=(a1,…,ap)∈(ℝn)p\bm{a}=(a_{1},\dots,a_{p})\in(\mathbb{R}^{n})^{p}, are homothetic. Denote ρ𝒕:=∑l=0ptl−1\rho_{\bm{t}}:=\sum_{l=0}^{p}t_{l}^{-1}. Since

Hp,𝒕,K∩(E𝒕+(0,0,𝒂))\displaystyle H_{p,\bm{t},K}\cap\big(E_{\bm{t}}+(0,0,\bm{a})\big) ={(θ^𝒕,ρ𝒕−1x,𝒂):x∈K,ρ𝒕𝒂∈−Δp(x)+Kp}\displaystyle=\left\{\left(\hat{\theta}_{\bm{t}},\rho_{\bm{t}}^{-1}x,\bm{a}\right)\,:\,x\in K,\rho_{\bm{t}}\bm{a}\in-\Delta_{p}(x)+K^{p}\right\}
={(θ^𝒕,y,𝒂):y∈ρ𝒕−1​K∩⋂l=1p(ρ𝒕−1​K−al)}\displaystyle=\left\{(\hat{\theta}_{\bm{t}},y,\bm{a})\,:\,y\in\rho_{\bm{t}}^{-1}K\cap\bigcap_{l=1}^{p}\left(\rho_{\bm{t}}^{-1}K-a_{l}\right)\right\}
={θ𝒕}×(ρ𝒕−1​K∩⋂l=1p(ρ𝒕−1​K−al))×{𝒂},\displaystyle=\{\theta_{\bm{t}}\}\times\left(\rho_{\bm{t}}^{-1}K\cap\bigcap_{l=1}^{p}\left(\rho_{\bm{t}}^{-1}K-a_{l}\right)\right)\times\{\bm{a}\},

it follow that the bodies

ρ𝒕−1​K∩⋂l=1p(ρ𝒕−1​K−al),𝒂∈ρ𝒕−1​(Dp​K),\rho_{\bm{t}}^{-1}K\cap\bigcap_{l=1}^{p}\left(\rho_{\bm{t}}^{-1}K-a_{l}\right),\quad\bm{a}\in\rho_{\bm{t}}^{-1}(D_{p}K),

are all mutually homothetic. By Corollary 2.4, KK thus has to be a simplex. ∎

Observe that Conjecture 1.3, if true, clearly implies Theorem 7.3. It is also easy to see that equality holds in (28) for any K∈𝒦⁡(ℝn)K\in\mathcal{K}(\mathbb{R}^{n}) if 𝒕\bm{t} lies on the relative boundary of Θp\Theta_{p}. Finally, integrating (28) with respect to 𝒕\bm{t} over the set Θp\Theta_{p} at once yields the following corollary, analogous to Corollary 1.6:

Corollary 7.4.

Let p∈ℕp\in\mathbb{N}. For any K∈𝒦⁡(ℝn)K\in\mathcal{K}(\mathbb{R}^{n}), one has

∑𝒋∈𝒥pn(n​pn−𝒋)−1​Wp,K​(𝒋)≤(n!)p(n​p)!​∑𝒋∈𝒥pn(n​pn−𝒋)−1​(n𝒋)​|K|p.\displaystyle\sum_{\bm{j}\in\mathcal{J}^{n}_{p}}{np\choose n-\bm{j}}^{-1}W_{p,K}(\bm{j})\leq\frac{(n!)^{p}}{(np)!}\sum_{\bm{j}\in\mathcal{J}^{n}_{p}}{np\choose n-\bm{j}}^{-1}{n\choose\bm{j}}|K|^{p}.

7.2. Weighted inequalities III

Here we prove a different weighted inequality for mixed volumes of −Δp​K-\Delta_{p}K and ι1​K,…,ιp​K\iota_{1}K,\dots,\iota_{p}K, analogous to Theorem 1.7. Let us start by introducing the corresponding higher-order generalization of unbalanced difference body, since it will play a role in the proof. Let p∈ℕp\in\mathbb{N}. For any 𝒕=(t0,…,tp)∈Θp\bm{t}=(t_{0},\dots,t_{p})\in\Theta_{p} and K∈𝒦⁡(ℝn)K\in\mathcal{K}(\mathbb{R}^{n}) we define

Dp𝒕​K:=−t0​Δp​K+∑l=1ptl​ιl​K.D_{p}^{\bm{t}}K:=-t_{0}\Delta_{p}K+\sum_{l=1}^{p}t_{l}\iota_{l}K.

Observe that, for p=1p=1, D1(t0,1−t0)​K=Dt0​KD_{1}^{(t_{0},1-t_{0})}K=D^{t_{0}}K agrees with the unbalanced difference body defined by Artstein-Avidan and Putterman [2]. Moire details about the body Dp𝒕​KD_{p}^{\bm{t}}K will be given and the corresponding Schneider–Rogers–Shephard type inequality will be conjectured in §7.3.

Lemma 7.5.

Let p∈ℕp\in\mathbb{N}, K∈𝒦⁡(ℝn)K\in\mathcal{K}(\mathbb{R}^{n}) with dimK=n\dim K=n, and let 𝐭∈relint⁡(Θp)\bm{t}\in\relint(\Theta_{p}) be such that t0=min⁡{t0,…,tp}t_{0}=\min\{t_{0},\dots,t_{p}\}. The function

f𝒕,K​(𝒙):=|t0​K|−1​|(t0​K)∩(t1​K−x1)∩⋯∩(tp​K−xp)|,𝒙=(x1,…,xp)∈(ℝn)p,f_{\bm{t},K}(\bm{x}):=|t_{0}K|^{-1}\,\big|(t_{0}K)\cap(t_{1}K-x_{1})\cap\cdots\cap(t_{p}K-x_{p})\big|,\quad\bm{x}=(x_{1},\dots,x_{p})\in(\mathbb{R}^{n})^{p},

is continuous and satisfies the following properties:

  1. (a)

    ∫ℝn​pf𝒕,K​(𝒙)​d​𝒙=|K|p​∏l=1ptln\int_{\mathbb{R}^{np}}f_{\bm{t},K}(\bm{x})\,\textup{d}\bm{x}=|K|^{p}\prod_{l=1}^{p}t_{l}^{n}.

  2. (b)

    supp⁡f𝒕,K=Dp𝒕​K\supp f_{\bm{t},K}=D_{p}^{\bm{t}}K.

  3. (c)

    f𝒕,K​(ℝn​p)=[0,1]f_{\bm{t},K}(\mathbb{R}^{np})=[0,1]. Moreover, f𝒕,K​(𝒙)=0f_{\bm{t},K}(\bm{x})=0 if and only if 𝒙∉int⁡(Dp𝐭​K)\bm{x}\notin\inter(D_{p}^{\bm{t}}K), and f𝒕,K​(𝒙)=1f_{\bm{t},K}(\bm{x})=1 if and only if 𝒙∈∑l=1p(tl−t0)​ιl​K.\bm{x}\in\sum_{l=1}^{p}(t_{l}-t_{0})\iota_{l}K.

  4. (d)

    For any 𝒚,𝒛∈Dp𝒕​K\bm{y},\bm{z}\in D_{p}^{\bm{t}}K and s∈[0,1]s\in[0,1], it holds that

    f𝒕,K​((1−s)​𝒚+s​𝒛)1n≥(1−s)​f𝒕,K​(𝒚)1n+s​f𝒕,K​(𝒛)1n.f_{\bm{t},K}\big((1-s)\bm{y}+s\bm{z}\big)^{\frac{1}{n}}\geq(1-s)f_{\bm{t},K}(\bm{y})^{\frac{1}{n}}+sf_{\bm{t},K}(\bm{z})^{\frac{1}{n}}.
Proof.

First, continuity is clear. Second, (a) follows easily from Fubini’s theorem since

∫ℝn​pf𝒕,K​(𝒙)​d​𝒙\displaystyle\int_{\mathbb{R}^{np}}f_{\bm{t},K}(\bm{x})\,\textup{d}\bm{x} =|t0​K|−1​∫ℝn​p|(t0​K)∩(t1​K−x1)∩⋯∩(tp​K−xp)|​d​𝒙\displaystyle=|t_{0}K|^{-1}\int_{\mathbb{R}^{np}}\big|(t_{0}K)\cap(t_{1}K-x_{1})\cap\cdots\cap(t_{p}K-x_{p})\big|\,\textup{d}\bm{x}
=|t0​K|−1​∫ℝn​p∫ℝnχt0​K​(x0)​∏l=1pχtl​K​(x0+xl)​d​x0​d​𝒙\displaystyle=|t_{0}K|^{-1}\int_{\mathbb{R}^{np}}\int_{\mathbb{R}^{n}}\chi_{t_{0}K}(x_{0})\prod_{l=1}^{p}\chi_{t_{l}K}(x_{0}+x_{l})\,\textup{d}x_{0}\,\textup{d}\bm{x}
=|t0​K|−1​∫ℝnχt0​K​(x0)​(∏l=1p∫ℝnχtl​K​(x0+xl)​d​xl)​d​x0\displaystyle=|t_{0}K|^{-1}\int_{\mathbb{R}^{n}}\chi_{t_{0}K}(x_{0})\left(\prod_{l=1}^{p}\int_{\mathbb{R}^{n}}\chi_{t_{l}K}(x_{0}+x_{l})\,\textup{d}x_{l}\right)\,\textup{d}x_{0}
=|t0​K|−1​(∏l=1ptln)​|K|p​∫ℝnχt0​K​(x0)​d​x0\displaystyle=|t_{0}K|^{-1}\left(\prod_{l=1}^{p}t_{l}^{n}\right)|K|^{p}\int_{\mathbb{R}^{n}}\chi_{t_{0}K}(x_{0})\,\textup{d}x_{0}
=|K|p​∏l=1ptln.\displaystyle=|K|^{p}\prod_{l=1}^{p}t_{l}^{n}.

Third, it is straightforward to verify, cf. proof of [11, Proposition 3.1], that

Dp𝒕​K={𝒙∈(ℝn)p:t0​K∩(t1​K−x1)∩⋯∩(tp​K−xp)≠∅}.D_{p}^{\bm{t}}K=\left\{\bm{x}\in(\mathbb{R}^{n})^{p}\,:\,t_{0}K\cap(t_{1}K-x_{1})\cap\cdots\cap(t_{p}K-x_{p})\neq\emptyset\right\}.

This immediately implies (b) and the second part of (c). Since clearly f𝒕,K​(ℝn​p)⊂[0,1]f_{\bm{t},K}(\mathbb{R}^{np})\subset[0,1], the first part of (c) follows by continuity. Finally, to prove (d), notice first that we have

(t0​K)∩⋂l=1p(tl​K−((1−s)​yl+s​zl))\displaystyle(t_{0}K)\cap\bigcap_{l=1}^{p}\Big(t_{l}K-\big((1-s)y_{l}+sz_{l}\big)\Big)
=((1−s)​t0​K+s​t0​K)∩⋂l=1p((1−s)​(tl​K−yl)+s⁡(tl​K−zl))\displaystyle\quad=\big((1-s)t_{0}K+st_{0}K\big)\cap\bigcap_{l=1}^{p}\big((1-s)(t_{l}K-y_{l})+s(t_{l}K-z_{l})\big)
⊇(1−s)​((t0​K)∩⋂l=1p(tl​K−yl))+s⁡((t0​K)∩⋂l=1p(tl​K−zl)).\displaystyle\quad\supseteq(1-s)\big((t_{0}K)\cap\bigcap_{l=1}^{p}(t_{l}K-y_{l})\big)+s\big((t_{0}K)\cap\bigcap_{l=1}^{p}(t_{l}K-z_{l})\big).

This and the Brunn–Minkowski inequality (Theorem 2.2) readily imply the claim. ∎

Theorem 7.6.

Let p∈ℕp\in\mathbb{N}. For any K∈𝒦⁡(ℝn)K\in\mathcal{K}(\mathbb{R}^{n}) and 𝐭∈Θp\bm{t}\in\Theta_{p}, one has

(29) ∑𝒋∈𝒥pnqn,p,𝒋​(𝒕)​Wp,K​(𝒋)≤𝒕n​|K|p,\displaystyle\sum_{\bm{j}\in\mathcal{J}^{n}_{p}}q_{n,p,\bm{j}}(\bm{t})W_{p,K}(\bm{j})\leq\bm{t}^{n}|K|^{p},

where, denoting tmin:=min⁡{t0,…,tp}t_{\min}:=\min\{t_{0},\dots,t_{p}\}, we set

qn,p,𝒋​(𝒕):=n​(tmin)n​(n​pn−𝒋)​∫01(1−s)n−1​∏l=0p(tl−(1−s)​tmin)n−jl​d​s.q_{n,p,\bm{j}}(\bm{t}):=n(t_{\min})^{n}{np\choose n-\bm{j}}\int_{0}^{1}(1-s)^{n-1}\prod_{l=0}^{p}\big(t_{l}-(1-s)t_{\min}\big)^{n-j_{l}}\,\textup{d}s.

If dim(K)=n\dim(K)=n and equality in (29) holds for some 𝐭∈relint⁡(Θp)\bm{t}\in\relint(\Theta_{p}), then KK is a simplex.

Proof.

It suffices to prove (29) for KK with dim(K)=n\dim(K)=n and for 𝒕∈relint⁡(Θp)\bm{t}\in\relint(\Theta_{p}). Without loss of generality we may also assume that tmin=t0t_{\min}=t_{0}. Then one has the decomposition

(30) Dp𝒕​K=K𝒕+K𝒕′,\displaystyle D_{p}^{\bm{t}}K=K_{\bm{t}}+K^{\prime}_{\bm{t}},

where K𝒕:=∑l=1p(tl−t0)​ιl​KK_{\bm{t}}:=\sum_{l=1}^{p}(t_{l}-t_{0})\iota_{l}K and K𝒕′:=t0​Dp​KK^{\prime}_{\bm{t}}:=t_{0}D_{p}K. For any 𝒙∈Dp𝒕​K\bm{x}\in D_{p}^{\bm{t}}K we set

s𝒙:=min⁡{s∈[0,1]:𝒙=(1−s)​𝒚+s​𝒛​ for some ​𝒚∈K𝒕​ and ​𝒛∈Dp𝒕​K}.s_{\bm{x}}:=\min\big\{s\in[0,1]\,:\,\bm{x}=(1-s)\bm{y}+s\bm{z}\text{ for some }\bm{y}\in K_{\bm{t}}\text{ and }\bm{z}\in D_{p}^{\bm{t}}K\big\}.

It holds

(31) s𝒙=dK𝒕′​(𝒙,K𝒕).s_{\bm{x}}=d_{K^{\prime}_{\bm{t}}}(\bm{x},K_{\bm{t}}).

Indeed, set ρ≔dK𝒕′​(𝒙,K𝒕)=min⁡{r≥0:𝒙∈K𝒕+r​K𝒕′}\rho\coloneqq d_{K^{\prime}_{\bm{t}}}(\bm{x},K_{\bm{t}})=\min\{r\geq 0:\bm{x}\in K_{\bm{t}}+rK^{\prime}_{\bm{t}}\} and observe that (30) implies that ρ∈[0,1]\rho\in[0,1]. Proof of Theorem 1.7.

7.3. Higher-order unbalanced difference body II

Recall from §7.2 that we define for p∈ℕp\in\mathbb{N} and 𝒕=(t0,…,tp)∈Θp\bm{t}=(t_{0},\dots,t_{p})\in\Theta_{p} the higher-order unbalanced difference body of K∈𝒦⁡(ℝn)K\in\mathcal{K}(\mathbb{R}^{n}) as

Motivated by [2, Conjecture 2], we conjecture the corresponding unbalanced Schneider–Rogers–Shephard type inequality, analogous to Conjecture 1.8:

Let p∈ℕp\in\mathbb{N}. For any K∈𝒦⁡(ℝn)K\in\mathcal{K}(\mathbb{R}^{n}) with dim(K)=n\dim(K)=n and any 𝐭∈Θp\bm{t}\in\Theta_{p}, one has

where Sn∈𝒦⁡(ℝn)S_{n}\in\mathcal{K}(\mathbb{R}^{n}) is an nn-simplex. If equality holds for some t∈relint⁡(Θp)t\in\relint(\Theta_{p}), then KK is a simplex.

∑𝒋∈𝒥pn(n​pn−𝒋)𝒕n−𝒋Wp,K(𝒋)≤∑𝒋∈𝒥pn(nj0)⋯(njp)𝒕n−𝒋|K|p,𝒕∈Θp.\sum_{\bm{j}\in\mathcal{J}^{n}_{p}}{np\choose n-\bm{j}}\bm{t}^{n-\bm{j}}W_{p,K}(\bm{j})\leq\sum_{\bm{j}\in\mathcal{J}^{n}_{p}}{n\choose j_{0}}\cdots{n\choose j_{p}}\bm{t}^{n-\bm{j}}|K|^{p},\quad\bm{t}\in\Theta_{p}.

In this formulation it is obvious that Conjecture 7.7 would follow from Conjecture 1.3. Moreover, by the same considerations as in the proof of Theorem 1.7, it is easily seen that Conjecture 7.7 implies Conjecture 1.8. Let us show that Conjecture 7.7, if true, directly implies the weighted inequalities proven in Theorems 7.3 and 7.6.

Lemma 8.2.

Let p∈ℕp\in\mathbb{N}, t∈[0,1]t\in[0,1], and let Sn∈𝒦⁡(ℝn)S_{n}\in\mathcal{K}(\mathbb{R}^{n}) be an nn-simplex.

  1. (a)

    If SnS_{n} is centered, then

    |Qp,t,Sn|=(nk)​(1−t)n​p−k​tk​|Sn|p,\displaystyle|Q_{p,t,S_{n}}|={n\choose k}(1-t)^{np-k}t^{k}|S_{n}|^{p},
  2. (b)

    If 00 is a vertex of SnS_{n}, then

    |Qp,t,Sn|=(1−t)n⁡(p−1)​|Sn|p.\displaystyle|Q_{p,t,S_{n}}|=(1-t)^{n(p-1)}|S_{n}|^{p}.
Proof.

The case p=1p=1 was proven in [1, Lemma 2.1 and §5.4]. The general case then follows at once from Lemma 8.1. ∎

Now we can proceed to the proof of our main result.

Proof of Theorem 1.9.

Fix t∈[0,1]t\in[0,1] and K∈𝒦⁡(ℝn)K\in\mathcal{K}(\mathbb{R}^{n}) with 0∈K0\in K. Consider the subspace E:=ℝ×{0}⊂ℝ×ℝn​pE:=\mathbb{R}\times\{0\}\subset\mathbb{R}\times\mathbb{R}^{np}. Since 0∈K0\in K, we have E∩Cp,t,K=[0,1]E\cap C_{p,t,K}=[0,1]. Using this and PE⟂​Cp,t,k=Qp,t,KP_{E^{\perp}}C_{p,t,k}=Q_{p,t,K}, Lemmas 2.1 and 6.2 imply

|Qp,t,K|≤(n​p+11)​|Cp,t,K|=(n​p+1)​|Cp,t,K|≤(1−t)n⁡(p−1)​|K|p,\displaystyle|Q_{p,t,K}|\leq{np+1\choose 1}|C_{p,t,K}|=(np+1)|C_{p,t,K}|\leq(1-t)^{n(p-1)}|K|^{p},

proving (9).

Assume that dimK=n\dim K=n and that equality holds in (9) for some t∈(0,1)t\in(0,1). Then we in particular have equality in (19). Since (19) was the only inequality used in the proof of Theorem 1.5, we in turn have equality in (6) and hence Theorem 1.5 implies that KK is a simplex.

By Lemma 8.1, any nn-simplex satisfying equality in (9) satisfies equality in (9) for p=1p=1. It was shown in [1, §5.4] that in such a case, the simplex must have a vertex at the origin. This finishes the proof. ∎

Proof of Corollary 1.10.

We may assume 0∈K0\in K. Let t∈(0,1)t\in(0,1). Theorem 1.9 together with the monotonicity of mixed volume applied to (1−t)​Kp⊂Qp,t,K(1-t)K^{p}\subset Q_{p,t,K} and −t​Δp​K⊂Qp,t,K-t\Delta_{p}K\subset Q_{p,t,K} implies

Vn​p​(Kp​[n​p−j],−Δp​K​[j])≤|Qp,t,K|tj​(1−t)n​p−j≤|K|ptj​(1−t)n−j.\displaystyle V_{np}(K^{p}[np-j],-\Delta_{p}K[j])\leq\frac{|Q_{p,t,K}|}{t^{j}(1-t)^{np-j}}\leq\frac{|K|^{p}}{t^{j}(1-t)^{n-j}}.

Choosing t=jnt=\frac{j}{n} yields the result. ∎

To conclude this section, we will show that the corresponding Fáry–Rédei type conjecture (Conjecture 1.11) implies the inequality part of Conjecture 1.2.

Proposition 8.3.

Conjecture 1.11 implies inequality (4) in Conjecture 1.2.

Proof.

Let p∈ℕp\in\mathbb{N}, 1≤j≤n1\leq j\leq n, and assume that K∈𝒦⁡(ℝn)K\in\mathcal{K}(\mathbb{R}^{n}) with dimK=n\dim K=n satisfies Conjecture 1.11. Set t:=jn+1t:=\frac{j}{n+1} and let x∈Kx\in K be such that

|Qp,t,K−x||K|p≤|Qp,t,Sn||Sn|p.\frac{|Q_{p,t,K-x}|}{|K|^{p}}\leq\frac{|Q_{p,t,S_{n}}|}{|S_{n}|^{p}}.

Then, using Lemma 8.2 together with the monotonicity and translation invariance of mixed volumes, we obtain

Vn​p​(Kp​[n​p−j],−Δp​K​[j])≤|Qp,t,K−x|(1−t)n​p−j​tj≤|Qp,t,Sn|(1−t)n​p−j​tj​|Sn|p​|K|p=(nj)​|K|p.\displaystyle V_{np}(K^{p}[np-j],-\Delta_{p}K[j])\leq\frac{|Q_{p,t,K-x}|}{(1-t)^{np-j}t^{j}}\leq\frac{|Q_{p,t,S_{n}}|}{(1-t)^{np-j}t^{j}|S_{n}|^{p}}|K|^{p}={n\choose j}|K|^{p}.

∎

9. Inequalities for the unbalanced join of −Δp​K-\Delta_{p}K and ι1​K,…,ιp​K\iota_{1}K,\dots,\iota_{p}K

In this last section, we consider the unbalanced join of the bodies −Δp​K-\Delta_{p}K and ι1​K,…,ιp​K\iota_{1}K,\dots,\iota_{p}K for K∈𝒦⁡(ℝn)K\in\mathcal{K}(\mathbb{R}^{n}) and generalize the results of the previous section to this setting, that is, to the context of Conjecture 1.3. First, we will prove a sharp upper bound for the volume of this join (Theorem 9.1) which in particular implies the currently best known general upper bound on the mixed volume of the respective convex bodies (Corollary 9.2). Then we formulate the corresponding Fáry–Rédei type conjecture (Conjecture 9.3) and prove that it implies the inequality part of Conjecture 1.3.

Recall that we keep the notation established above, in particular in Sections 3 and 7. Analogously to Section 8, for any p∈ℕp\in\mathbb{N}, 𝒕∈Θp\bm{t}\in\Theta_{p}, and K∈𝒦⁡(ℝn)K\in\mathcal{K}(\mathbb{R}^{n}) we set

Rp,𝒕,K:=−t0​Δp​K∨⋁l=1ptl​ιl​K.R_{p,\bm{t},K}:=-t_{0}\Delta_{p}K\vee\bigvee_{l=1}^{p}t_{l}\iota_{l}K.

Then for E:={0}×ℝn​p⊂ℝp×ℝn​pE:=\{0\}\times\mathbb{R}^{np}\subset\mathbb{R}^{p}\times\mathbb{R}^{np} we have PE​(Gp,𝒕,K)=Rp,𝒕,KP_{E}(G_{p,\bm{t},K})=R_{p,\bm{t},K}, see (23). This observation will be used in the proof of the upper bound for Rp,𝒕,KR_{p,\bm{t},K}. Since no analog of Lemma 8.1 is known to us in this setting, the last part of the proof of the following theorem cannot be reduced to the case p=1p=1 proven in [1, §5.4]; instead, we will use a different argument to show directly that if a simplex attains equality, it must have a vertex at the origin.

Theorem 9.1.

Let p∈ℕp\in\mathbb{N}. For any K∈𝒦⁡(ℝn)K\in\mathcal{K}(\mathbb{R}^{n}) with 0∈K0\in K and any 𝐭∈Θp\bm{t}\in\Theta_{p}, one has

(42) |Rp,𝒕,K|≤(n!)p(n​p)!​∑𝒋∈𝒥pn(n𝒋)​𝒕n−𝒋​|K|p.\displaystyle|R_{p,\bm{t},K}|\leq\frac{(n!)^{p}}{(np)!}\sum_{\bm{j}\in\mathcal{J}^{n}_{p}}{n\choose\bm{j}}\bm{t}^{n-\bm{j}}|K|^{p}.

If dim(K)=n\dim(K)=n and equality holds for some 𝐭∈relint⁡(Θp)\bm{t}\in\relint(\Theta_{p}), then KK is a simplex with a vertex at the origin.

Proof.

Fix 𝒕∈Θp\bm{t}\in\Theta_{p} and K∈𝒦⁡(ℝn)K\in\mathcal{K}(\mathbb{R}^{n}) with 0∈K0\in K. Consider the subspace E:=ℝp×{0}⊂ℝp×ℝn​pE:=\mathbb{R}^{p}\times\{0\}\subset\mathbb{R}^{p}\times\mathbb{R}^{np}. Since 0∈K0\in K, we have E∩Gp,𝒕,K=Θ^pE\cap G_{p,\bm{t},K}=\hat{\Theta}_{p}; in particular |E∩Gp,𝒕,K|=1p!|E\cap G_{p,\bm{t},K}|=\frac{1}{p!}. Using this and PE⟂​Gp,𝒕,k=Rp,𝒕,KP_{E^{\perp}}G_{p,\bm{t},k}=R_{p,\bm{t},K}, Lemmas 2.1 and 7.2 imply

|Rp,𝒕,K|≤p!​(n​p+pp)​|Gp,𝒕,K|=(n​p+p)!(n​p)!​|Gp,𝒕,K|≤(n!)p(n​p)!​∑𝒋∈𝒥pn(n𝒋)​𝒕n−𝒋​|K|p,\displaystyle|R_{p,\bm{t},K}|\leq p!{np+p\choose p}|G_{p,\bm{t},K}|=\frac{(np+p)!}{(np)!}|G_{p,\bm{t},K}|\leq\frac{(n!)^{p}}{(np)!}\sum_{\bm{j}\in\mathcal{J}^{n}_{p}}{n\choose\bm{j}}\bm{t}^{n-\bm{j}}|K|^{p},

proving (42).

Assume that dimK=n\dim K=n and that equality holds in (42) for some 𝒕∈relint⁡(Θp)\bm{t}\in\relint(\Theta_{p}). First, we in particular have equality in (26). Since (26) was the only inequality used in the proof of Theorem 7.3, we in turn have equality in (28) and hence Theorem 7.3 implies that KK is a simplex.

Second, equality in the application of Lemma 2.1 implies that the bodies

S𝒂:={s^∈Θ^p:(𝒔^,𝒂)∈Gp,𝒕,K},𝒂∈E⟂,S_{\bm{a}}:=\big\{\hat{s}\in\hat{\Theta}_{p}:(\hat{\bm{s}},\bm{a})\in G_{p,\bm{t},K}\big\},\quad\bm{a}\in E^{\perp},

are all homothetic to Gp,𝒕,K∩E=Θ^pG_{p,\bm{t},K}\cap E=\hat{\Theta}_{p}. Let K=conv⁡{v0,…,vn}K=\conv\{v_{0},\dots,v_{n}\} and let Aj​(x)=αj​(x)+βjA_{j}(x)=\alpha_{j}(x)+\beta_{j} for x∈ℝnx\in\mathbb{R}^{n} and j=0,…,nj=0,\dots,n be as in §2.3, that is, ∑j=0nAj​(x)=1\sum_{j=0}^{n}A_{j}(x)=1, x∈ℝnx\in\mathbb{R}^{n}, Aj​(vi)=δi​jA_{j}(v_{i})=\delta_{ij}, and

(43) K={x∈ℝn:Aj(x)≥0,j=0,…,n}.\displaystyle K=\{x\in\mathbb{R}^{n}:A_{j}(x)\geq 0,\,j=0,\dots,n\}.

Since 0∈K0\in K, we have βj=Aj​(0)≥0\beta_{j}=A_{j}(0)\geq 0 for j=0,…,nj=0,\dots,n. Moreover, ∑j=0nβj=1\sum_{j=0}^{n}\beta_{j}=1 and ∑j=0nαj=0\sum_{j=0}^{n}\alpha_{j}=0. Observe also that α1,…,αn\alpha_{1},\dots,\alpha_{n} are linearly independent.

We claim that

(44) S𝒂={𝒔^∈Θ^p:∑j=0nmj​(𝒂,𝒔)≤0},\displaystyle S_{\bm{a}}=\left\{\hat{\bm{s}}\in\hat{\Theta}_{p}\,:\,\sum_{j=0}^{n}m_{j}(\bm{a},\bm{s})\leq 0\right\},

where

mj(𝒂,𝒔)≔max{−s0t0βj,−αj(a1)−s1t1βj,…,−αj(ap)−sptpβj},j=0,…,n.m_{j}(\bm{a},\bm{s})\coloneqq\max\big\{-s_{0}t_{0}\beta_{j},-\alpha_{j}(a_{1})-s_{1}t_{1}\beta_{j},\dots,-\alpha_{j}(a_{p})-s_{p}t_{p}\beta_{j}\big\},\quad j=0,\dots,n.

To prove this, observe first that 𝒔^∈S𝒂\hat{\bm{s}}\in S_{\bm{a}} if and only if 𝒂=−s0​t0​Δp​(x)+∑l=1psl​tl​ιl​(yl)\bm{a}=-s_{0}t_{0}\Delta_{p}(x)+\sum_{l=1}^{p}s_{l}t_{l}\iota_{l}(y_{l}) for some x,y1,…,yp∈Kx,y_{1},\dots,y_{p}\in K or, equivalently, if and only if there exists

u∈s0​t0​K∩⋂l=1p(sl​tl​K−al).u\in s_{0}t_{0}K\cap\bigcap_{l=1}^{p}(s_{l}t_{l}K-a_{l}).

By (43), this in turn is equivalent to the existence of u∈ℝnu\in\mathbb{R}^{n} satisfying

One the one hand, because ∑j=0nαj=0\sum_{j=0}^{n}\alpha_{j}=0, (45) implies ∑j=0nmj​(𝒂,𝒔)≤0\sum_{j=0}^{n}m_{j}(\bm{a},\bm{s})\leq 0. Conversely, if ∑j=0nmj​(𝒂,𝒔)≤0\sum_{j=0}^{n}m_{j}(\bm{a},\bm{s})\leq 0, then one can choose numbers r0,…,rnr_{0},\dots,r_{n} such that rj≥mj​(𝒂,𝒔)r_{j}\geq m_{j}(\bm{a},\bm{s}) for all jj and ∑j=0nrj=0\sum_{j=0}^{n}r_{j}=0. Since α1,…,αn\alpha_{1},\dots,\alpha_{n} are linearly independent and ∑j=0nαj=0\sum_{j=0}^{n}\alpha_{j}=0, there exists u∈ℝnu\in\mathbb{R}^{n} such that αj​(u)=rj≥mj​(𝒂,𝒔)\alpha_{j}(u)=r_{j}\geq m_{j}(\bm{a},\bm{s}) for every jj. Hence 𝒔∈S𝒂\bm{s}\in S_{\bm{a}} and (44) follows.

Assume that 00 is not a vertex of KK. Since ∑j=0nβj=1\sum_{j=0}^{n}\beta_{j}=1, at least two of the numbers β0,…,βn≥0\beta_{0},\dots,\beta_{n}\geq 0 are strictly positive; in particular, there exists i∈{0,…,n}i\in\{0,\dots,n\} with βi∈(0,1)\beta_{i}\in(0,1). Let q,ε2,…,εp>0q,\varepsilon_{2},\dots,\varepsilon_{p}>0 be such that

q​∑l=0ptl−1<1and∑l=2pεl=1−q​∑l=0ptl−1.q\sum_{l=0}^{p}t_{l}^{-1}<1\qquad\text{and}\qquad\sum_{l=2}^{p}\varepsilon_{l}=1-q\sum_{l=0}^{p}t_{l}^{-1}.

First, if j=ij=i, we have

−αi​(a1)−s1∗​t1​βi=−q−q​βi<−q​βi=−s0∗​t0​βi,-\alpha_{i}(a_{1})-s_{1}^{*}t_{1}\beta_{i}=-q-q\beta_{i}<-q\beta_{i}=-s_{0}^{*}t_{0}\beta_{i},

and

−αj​(a1)−s1∗​t1​βj=qn−q​βj>−q​βj=−s0∗​t0​βj,-\alpha_{j}(a_{1})-s_{1}^{*}t_{1}\beta_{j}=\frac{q}{n}-q\beta_{j}>-q\beta_{j}=-s_{0}^{*}t_{0}\beta_{j},

and

mj​(𝒂∗,𝒔∗)=−αj​(a1)−s1∗​t1​βj.m_{j}(\bm{a}^{*},\bm{s}^{*})=-\alpha_{j}(a_{1})-s_{1}^{*}t_{1}\beta_{j}.

Since all of the above inequalities are strict, there exists a relatively open neighborhood U⊂relint⁡(Θp)U\subset\relint(\Theta_{p}) of 𝒔∗\bm{s}^{*} such that for all 𝒔∈U\bm{s}\in U we have

∑j=0nmj​(𝒂∗,𝒔)=−s0​t0​βi+∑j≠i(−αj​(a1)−s1​t1​βj).\sum_{j=0}^{n}m_{j}(\bm{a}^{*},\bm{s})=-s_{0}t_{0}\beta_{i}+\sum_{j\neq i}\big(-\alpha_{j}(a_{1})-s_{1}t_{1}\beta_{j}\big).
